## 2. Definitions

In what follows, we fix an algebraically closed field $K$ of arbitrary characteristic. If $v$ is a nonzero element in a vector space $V$ we write $\widetilde{v}$ for the image of $v$ in $\mathbb{P}(V)$ . We denote the projectivization of the vector space $\mathbb{A}^{k\times\ell}$ of $k\times\ell$ matrices by $\mathbb{P}^{k\times\ell-1}$ .

To help the reader locate relevant symbols, we have included the tables Table 1 and Table 2 in Appendix C.

### 2.1. Matrices, matroids and polytopes

Let $d$ and $n$ be integers. For a polytope $P$ , denote by ${\operatorname{Vert}}(P)$ the vertices of $P$ . The hypersimplex $\Delta_{d,n}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$ is defined by

$$ \Delta_{d,n}=\left\{(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in[0,1]^{n}\middle|\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}=d\right\}. $$

When $d$ and $n$ are clear from context, we sometimes write the hypersimplex as $\Delta$ rather than $\Delta_{d,n}$ . The hypersimplex is the convex hull of the vectors $e_{A}:=\sum_{i\in A}e_{i}$ , where $A$ ranges over all $d$ -element subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ . We will sometimes abuse notation and use the same symbol to denote both $e_{A}$ and $A$ .

Given a $d\times n$ matrix $M$ , we define the rank function ${\rm rk}_{M}:2^{\{1,\ldots,n\}}\to\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ by ${\rm rk}_{M}(A)={\rm rk}(M^{A})$ , where $M^{A}$ is the submatrix of $M$ formed by the columns in $A$ . When $M$ is clear from context, we sometimes write the rank function as ${\rm rk}$ rather than ${\rm rk}_{M}$ . The matroid of $M$ is the data of the rank function ${\rm rk}_{M}$ , which is determined by the maximal independent subsets of the columns of $M$ . The rank polytope of $M$ is the set

$$ P_{M}=\left\{(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\Delta_{d,n}\middle|\text{$\sum_{i\in A}x_{i}\leq{\rm rk}_{M}(A)$ for all $A\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}$}\right\} $$

and the independence polytope of $M$ is the set

$$ I_{M}=\left\{(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{n}\middle|\text{$\sum_{i\in A}x_{i}\leq{\rm rk}_{M}(A)$ for all $A\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}$}\right\}. $$

The rank polytope of $M$ is the convex hull of $e_{A}$ where $A$ ranges over all $d$ -element subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ such that ${\rm rk}_{M}(A)=d$ , and the independence polytope of $M$ is the convex hull of $e_{A}$ where $A$ ranges over all subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ such that ${\rm rk}_{M}(A)=|A|$ . The rank polytope of $M$ is empty if ${\rm rk}(M)<d$ and determines the matroid of $M$ if ${\rm rk}(M)=d$ . The rank polytope of a general $d\times n$ matrix is $\Delta_{d,n}$ .

As in [16], we say that a function $f$ from $d\times n$ matrices to an abelian group $Z$ is valuative (respectively additive) if whenever $\sum a_{i}1_{P_{M_{i}}}=0$ (respectively $\sum a_{i}1_{P_{M_{i}}}$ is supported on a positive codimension subset of $\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}=d\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$ ), we have $\sum a_{i}f(M_{i})=0$ . These notions have been intensely studied in a variety of contexts [15, 16, 49].

The following proposition shows we can replace the condition $\sum a_{i}1_{P_{M_{i}}}=0$ with the condition $\sum a_{i}1_{I_{M_{i}}}=0$ , which will be convenient at times.

#### Proposition 2.1.

For $d\times n$ matrices $M_{i}$ of rank $d$ , $\sum a_{i}1_{P_{M_{i}}}=0$ if and only if $\sum a_{i}1_{I_{M_{i}}}=0$ .

#### Proof.

If $\sum a_{i}1_{I_{M_{i}}}=0$ , then we can restrict to the hyperplane $\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}=d$ to obtain $\sum a_{i}1_{I_{M_{i}}}=0$ . Conversely, suppose $\sum a_{i}1_{P_{M_{i}}}=0$ . We recall that if $\{P_{i}\}$ is a collection of possibly unbounded polytopal regions, and $\sum a_{i}1_{P_{i}}=0$ , then $\sum a_{i}1_{R+P_{i}}=0$ for any ray $R$ (this can be checked on each ray parallel to $R$ separately). Applying this successively to $\sum a_{i}1_{P_{M_{i}}}=0$ with each of the negative coordinate rays and then restricting to the positive orthant yields $\sum a_{i}1_{I_{M_{i}}}=0$ . ∎

Parallel and series connection of matroids play a crucial role in this paper, and we recall the definition for matrices from [46, page 262, Figure 7.6(b)]. First, to simplify notation, we define the direct sum of two matrices.

#### Definition 2.1.

For matrices $M_{1},M_{2}$ , define the direct sum matrix $M_{1}\oplus M_{2}=\begin{pmatrix}M_{1}&0\\ 0&M_{2}\end{pmatrix}$ .

Let $M_{1}\in K^{d_{1}\times n_{1}}$ and $M_{2}\in K^{d_{2}\times n_{2}}$ . We now define the “parallel connection matrix” $P(M_{1},M_{2})$ and “series connection matrix” $S(M_{1},M_{2})$ (along the last column of $M_{1}$ and the first column of $M_{2}$ ). Definition 2.2 depends on certain non-canonical isomorphisms, so it only defines $P(M_{1},M_{2})$ and $S(M_{1},M_{2})$ up to left $GL$ -action.

#### Definition 2.2.

Let $W_{1}=K^{n_{1}}$ and $W_{2}=K^{n_{2}}$ . Let $x_{1,1},\ldots,x_{1,n_{1}}\in W_{1}$ be the columns of $M_{1}$ and let $x_{2,1},\ldots,x_{2,n_{2}}\in W_{2}$ be the columns of $M_{2}$ . The parallel connection matrix $P(M_{1},M_{2})\in K^{(d_{1}+d_{2}-1)\times(n_{1}+n_{2}-1)}$ is the matrix with columns $x_{1,1},\ldots,x_{1,n_{1}}=x_{2,1},\ldots,x_{2,n_{2}}$ , considered as elements of $(W_{1}\oplus W_{2})/\langle x_{1,n_{1}}-x_{2,1}\rangle\cong K^{n_{1}+n_{2}-1}$ . The series connection matrix $S(M_{1},M_{2})\in K^{(d_{1}+d_{2})\times(n_{1}+n_{2}-1)}$ is the matrix with columns $x_{1,1},\ldots,x_{1,n_{1}-1},x_{1,n_{1}}+x_{2,1},x_{2,2},\ldots,x_{2,n_{2}}$ , considered as elements of $W_{1}\oplus W_{2}\cong K^{n_{1}+n_{2}}$ .

If we consider a matrix as a collection of points in projective space, one point for each column, then series and parallel connection have intuitive geometric meanings.

Parallel connection (pictured on the left) corresponds to identifying two of the points. Series connection (pictured on the right) corresponds to drawing a line through two of the points and replacing them with a third (distinct) point on the connecting line.

#### Definition 2.3.

A series-parallel matrix is a matrix obtained from a general $1\times 1$ matrix by permutation of columns and series and parallel connection with general $1\times 2$ matrices.

Considering matrices as projective vector configurations, parallel connection with a general $1\times 2$ matrix corresponds to duplicating a vector, and series connection with a general $1\times 2$ matrix corresponds to removing a vector and sprouting off two general points on the line.

#### Definition 2.4.

We denote by $\ast$ a non-zero $1\times 1$ matrix.

We denote by $\tau^{\leq k}$ to be a general matrix with $k$ rows (where the number of columns will always be clear from context), a different general matrix every time it appears.

#### Definition 2.5.

A Schubert matroid $\operatorname{Sch}(r_{1},\ldots,r_{\ell},X_{1},\ldots,X_{\ell})$ with $\emptyset\subseteq X_{1}\subseteq\ldots\subseteq X_{\ell}=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and $0\leq r_{1}\leq\ldots\leq r_{\ell}=d$ is the matroid associated to a $d\times n$ matrix $M$ with the first $r_{i}$ entries of every column in $X_{i}\setminus X_{i-1}$ being general and the remaining entries being zero. Up to left $GL$ -action and column permutation, such a matrix can be written as

$$ \tau^{\leq r_{\ell}}(\tau^{\leq r_{\ell-1}}(\ldots\tau^{\leq r_{2}}(\tau^{\leq r_{1}}(\ast\oplus\ldots\oplus\ast)\oplus\ast\oplus\ldots\oplus\ast)\ldots)\oplus\ast\oplus\ldots\oplus\ast), $$

where the $\ast$ ’s in the $i$ ’th block from the left are associated to the indices in $X_{i}\setminus X_{i-1}$ .

In terms of point configurations, a Schubert matroid is given by fixing a flag, and picking general points in each member of the flag.

### 2.2. $GL_{r+1}$ -equivariant Chow rings

The standard references for equivariant intersection theory are [18, 19], see also [5] for a self-contained exposition. Let $t_{0},\ldots,t_{r}:(K^{\times})^{r+1}\to K^{\times}$ be the standard characters of the maximal torus $(K^{\times})^{r+1}$ of diagonal matrices in $GL_{r+1}$ . The $GL_{r+1}$ -equivariant Chow ring of a point is $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}({\rm pt})\cong\mathbb{Z}[t_{0},\ldots,t_{r}]^{S_{r+1}}$ [18, Section 3.2]. All tensor products $\otimes$ of equivariant Chow rings will be over $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}({\rm pt})$ .

We only consider varieties with algebraic cell decompositions, so $GL_{r+1}$ -equivariant Chow rings in this paper embed into the corresponding $(K^{\times})^{r+1}$ -equivariant Chow rings via the inclusion $\mathbb{Z}[t_{0},\ldots,t_{n}]^{S_{r+1}}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{Z}[t_{0},\ldots,t_{n}]$ . Thus we may treat the $t_{i}$ as separate variables.

The $GL_{r+1}$ -equivariant Chow ring of projective space is

$$ A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})=A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}({\rm pt})[H]/(F(H)) $$

where $H=c_{1}(\mathscr{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{r}}(1))$ and the degree $r+1$ polynomial $F(H)=\prod_{i=0}^{r}(H+t_{i})$ is the universal Leray relation [18, Section 3.3]. Also,

$$ A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}((\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n})=A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{\otimes n}=A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}({\rm pt})[H_{1},\ldots,H_{n}]/(F(H_{1}),\ldots,F(H_{n})) $$

and

$$ A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{(r+1)\times d-1})=A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}({\rm pt})[H]/(F(H)^{d}). $$

#### Definition 2.6.

For a one-variable polynomial $g$ with coefficients in $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}({\rm pt})$ , we define $\overline{g}$ to be the reduction of $g$ modulo $F$ (i.e. $\deg\overline{g}<\deg F$ and $g-\overline{g}$ is divisible by $F$ ).

If $g$ is a polynomial with coefficients in $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}({\rm pt})$ , then the equivariant integration (pushforward) map $\int_{\mathbb{P}^{r}}:A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})\to A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}({\rm pt})$ takes $g(H)$ to the coefficient of $H^{r}$ in $\bar{g}(H)$ .

#### Definition 2.7.

If $X$ is a variety acted on by $GL_{r+1}$ and $\alpha\in A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(X)$ , then we define the Kronecker dual $\alpha^{\dagger}$ as the function $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(X)\to A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}({\rm pt})$ given by

$$ \alpha^{\dagger}:\beta\mapsto\int\alpha\cap\beta. $$

### 2.3. The quantum product $\star$ and $QH^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})$

We define the small equivariant quantum cohomology ring of $\mathbb{P}^{r}$ (as an abstract ring, independent of characteristic) to be

$$ QH^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})=A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}({\rm pt})[z][\hbar]/(\hbar-F(z))\cong A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}({\rm pt})[z]. $$

Specializing to $\hbar=0$ recovers $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})$ , so $QH^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})$ is a commutative, associative deformation of $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})$ . We use $\star$ to denote the multiplication on $QH^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})$ .

If $f$ is a polynomial in one variable $z$ with coefficients in $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}({\rm pt})$ , we denote by $[z^{k}]f\in A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}({\rm pt})$ the coefficient of $z^{k}$ in $f$ . We denote by $[F(z)^{k}]f$ or $[\hbar^{k}]f$ the coefficient $a_{k}$ when $f$ is expressed as

$$ f(z)=a_{0}+a_{1}F(z)+a_{2}F(z)^{2}+\ldots=a_{0}+a_{1}\hbar+a_{2}\hbar^{2}+\ldots $$

where each coefficient $a_{i}$ is a polynomial of degree at most $r$ in $z$ .

#### 2.3.1. Quantum product $\star$ on $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})[\hbar]$

We will define an isomorphism of $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}({\rm pt})$ -modules between $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})[\hbar]$ and $H^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})$ and define $\star$ on $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})[\hbar]$ via this isomorphism.

There is an $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}({\rm pt})$ -linear lifting map

$$ \displaystyle A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r}) \displaystyle\to QH^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})\qquad\text{where }g(H)\mapsto\bar{g}(z), $$

given by choosing the representative that is reduced modulo $F$ . This yields an isomorphism $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})[\hbar]\cong QH^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})$ of $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}({\rm pt})$ -modules given by extending $\hbar$ -linearly. We use this isomorphism to define multiplication $\star$ on $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})[\hbar]$ . (Observe that $\star$ is not the usual multiplication operation on $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})[\hbar]$ as a polynomial ring over $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})$ .)

The operation $\star$ on $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})[\hbar]$ is $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}({\rm pt})[\hbar]$ -linear. If $f$ and $g$ are polynomials with coefficients in $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}({\rm pt})$ , then $f(H)\star g(H)=a(H)+b(H)\hbar$ , where $a$ and $b$ are the polynomials of degree at most $r$ with $\overline{f}(z)\overline{g}(z)=a(z)+b(z)F(z)$ . These two properties characterize the $\star$ -product. From an operational point of view, the usual multiplication on $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})$ is polynomial multiplication mod $F$ and the $\star$ -product is polynomial multiplication.

### 2.4. Generalized matrix orbit closures

Fix an integer $r$ . For each $d\times n$ matrix $M$ with no zero columns, we consider the map $\mu_{M}:\mathbb{P}^{(r+1)\times d-1}\dashrightarrow(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n}$ induced by multiplication $A\mapsto AM$ of $(r+1)\times d$ matrices with $M$ . More precisely, let $x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}$ be the columns of $M$ . Then $\mu_{M}(\widetilde{A})=(\widetilde{Ax_{1}},\ldots,\widetilde{Ax_{n}})\in(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{d}$ whenever $A\in\mathbb{A}^{(r+1)\times d}$ is a matrix such that $Ax_{i}\neq 0$ for all $i$ . The map $\mu_{M}$ is clearly $GL_{r+1}$ -equivariant. If $d\leq r+1$ , then $\overline{{\rm im}(\mu_{M})}$ is equal to the closure of the $GL_{r+1}$ -orbit of $(\widetilde{x}_{1},\ldots,\widetilde{x}_{n})\in(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n}$ , where $\widetilde{x_{i}}$ is considered in $\mathbb{P}^{r}$ via any linear inclusion $\mathbb{P}^{d-1}\subset\mathbb{P}^{r}$ . Let

be any resolution of the indeterminacy of $\mu_{M}$ . In proofs, we will always use the $GL_{r+1}$ -equivariant resolution given by the wonderful compactification of [41] detailed in Appendix B, which has the advantage of being given by a sequence of blowups along smooth centers.

We define the generalized matrix orbit of $M$ to be the algebraic cycle

$$ \mathcal{O}_{M}=(\widetilde{\mu}_{M})_{*}[B]=(\widetilde{\mu}_{M})_{*}\pi_{M}^{*}[\mathbb{P}^{(r+1)\times d-1}]\in Z_{(r+1)d-1}((\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n}). $$

This cycle is independent of the choice of resolution $\widetilde{\mu}_{M}$ , and is equal to $\overline{{\rm im}(\mu_{M})}$ or $0$ because if $\mu_{M}$ is generically finite then it is generically injective (if $\mu_{M}(A_{1})=\mu_{M}(A_{2})$ , then this further equals $\mu_{M}(A_{1}+tA_{2})$ for every $t$ ). We remark that this cycle is automatically $0$ if $d\geq n$ , however the graph closure $\overline{\Gamma_{M}}$ , which we will shortly define will be nontrivial even if $d\geq n$ . As the morphisms $\widetilde{\mu}_{M},\pi_{M}$ are $GL_{r+1}$ -equivariant we may further define the equivariant generalized matrix orbit pushforward and pullback maps

$$ (\mu_{M})_{*}:A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{(r+1)\times d-1})\rightleftarrows A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}((\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n}):\mu_{M}^{*} $$

on equivariant Chow groups by $(\mu_{M})_{*}=(\widetilde{\mu}_{M})_{*}\circ\pi_{M}^{*}$ and $\mu_{M}^{*}=(\pi_{M})_{*}\circ\widetilde{\mu}_{M}^{*}$ . These are $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}({\rm pt})$ -linear maps, independent of the choice of resolution. The graph closure $\overline{\Gamma_{M}}$ of $\mu_{M}$ is the $GL_{r+1}$ -equivariant cycle given by

$$ \overline{\Gamma_{M}}=\overline{\operatorname{im}(\operatorname{id}\times\mu_{M})}\in Z_{(r+1)d-1}(\mathbb{P}^{(r+1)\times d-1}\times(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n}), $$

and resolves the indeterminacy locus of $\mu_{M}$ via its two projections. We have

$$ \int_{\mathbb{P}^{(r+1)\times d-1}}\alpha\cap\mu_{M}^{*}\beta=\int_{B}\pi_{M}^{*}\alpha\cap\widetilde{\mu}_{M}^{*}\beta=\int_{(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n}}\beta\cap(\mu_{M})_{*}\alpha, $$

and $\int_{\overline{\Gamma_{M}}}\pi^{*}\alpha\cap\tilde{\mu}_{M}^{*}\beta=\int_{\mathbb{P}^{(r+1)\times d-1}\times(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n}}\alpha\cap\beta\cap[\overline{\Gamma_{M}}]$ , so the equivariant formulas for $(\mu_{M})_{*}$ , $\mu^{*}_{M}$ , and $[\overline{\Gamma_{M}}]$ all determine each other.

### 2.5. Class of an arbitrary orbit closure

Observe that since we defined $\mathcal{O}_{M}$ to be an $((r+1)d-1)$ -dimensional algebraic cycle, it does not contain the data of $\overline{{\rm im}(\mu_{M})}$ if $\dim(\overline{{\rm im}(\mu_{M})})<(r+1)d-1$ . This in particular occurs if $M$ is not a “connected” matrix. Nevertheless, for $d\leq r+1$ we can still write $\overline{{\rm im}(\mu_{M})}$ as the product of generalized matrix orbits as follows. First, by replacing $M$ with a subset of rows we may assume ${\rm rk}(M)=d$ .

#### Definition 2.8.

We say that a $d\times n$ matrix $M$ is connected if ${\rm rk}(M)=d$ and there does not exist $\varnothing\subsetneq A\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ such that ${\rm rk}_{M}(A)+{\rm rk}_{M}(\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus A)=d$ .

#### Example 1.

Any direct sum $M_{1}\oplus M_{2}$ is not connected. If $M$ is a general $d\times n$ matrix, then $M$ is connected if and only if $d<n$ .

Observe that any $d\times n$ matrix $M$ of rank $d$ with no zero columns can be written as

$$ g(M_{1}\oplus\ldots\oplus M_{k})P $$

where each $M_{i}$ is connected, $P$ is a permutation matrix, and $g\in GL_{d}$ .

#### Proposition 2.2.

Let $\widetilde{x}_{1},\ldots,\widetilde{x}_{n}\in\mathbb{P}^{d-1}$ be points not all contained in any hyperplane and let $M$ be the matrix with columns $x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}$ . Suppose that $M=M_{1}\oplus\cdots\oplus M_{k}$ where each $M_{i}$ is connected.

Then if $d\leq r+1$ , the $GL_{r+1}$ -orbit closure $\overline{{\rm im}(\mu_{M})}$ of $(\widetilde{x}_{1},\ldots,\widetilde{x}_{n})\in(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n}$ is equal to $\mathcal{O}_{M_{1}}\times\ldots\times\mathcal{O}_{M_{k}}$ and has the expected dimension $(r+1)d-k$ . Hence $[\overline{{\rm im}(\mu_{M})}]=\prod_{i=1}^{k}[\mathcal{O}_{M_{i}}]$ .

#### Proof.

We will first prove the proposition for $k=1$ . Viewing $\mathbb{P}^{d-1}$ as linearly embedded in $\mathbb{P}^{r}$ , it suffices to show that any element stabilizing $(\widetilde{x}_{1},\ldots,\widetilde{x}_{n})$ stabilizes every point of $\mathbb{P}^{d-1}$ . Indeed, given such a $g$ , each $x_{i}$ is an eigenvector of $g$ , so $K^{d}=\operatorname{Span}\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}$ is a direct sum of eigenspaces of $g$ . Since $M$ is connected, each $x_{i}$ has the same eigenvalue, so $g$ acts by a scalar on $K^{d}$ , as desired.

For any $k$ , let $d_{i}$ be the number of columns of $M_{i}$ . Then, if $A_{i}$ is a $(r+1)\times d_{i}$ matrix for $1\leq i\leq n$ , we have the equality of block matrices

$$ \begin{pmatrix}|&&|\\
A_{1}&\cdots&A_{k}\\
|&&|\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}M_{1}&&\\
&\ddots&\\
&&M_{k}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}|&&|\\
A_{1}M_{1}&\cdots&A_{k}M_{k}\\
|&&|\end{pmatrix}. $$

Hence $\overline{{\rm im}(\mu_{M})}=\overline{{\rm im}(\mu_{M_{1}})}\times\ldots\times\overline{{\rm im}(\mu_{M_{k}})}$ and the result follows from the previous paragraph. ∎

By the above, to compute the equivariant class of any $GL_{r+1}$ -orbit in $(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n}$ it suffices to compute the classes $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ . From now on we work exclusively with $\mathcal{O}_{M}$ instead of $\overline{{\rm im}(\mu_{M})}$ .

All of our theorems can be trivially extended to all matrices by defining $\mathcal{O}_{M}$ , $(\mu_{M})_{*}$ , $\mu_{M}^{*}$ , and $\overline{\Gamma_{M}}$ to all be zero if $M$ has a zero column. However, we will not treat matrices with a zero column in our proofs.

### 2.6. The operation $[M]_{\hbar}$

In this last subsection, we define our operation $[M]_{\hbar}$ for a $d\times n$ matrix $M$ . The operator

$$ [M]_{\hbar}:A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{\otimes n}\to QH^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r}) $$

is defined by taking the formal sum of convolutions (partial integrals to the last factor of $\mathbb{P}^{r}$ )

$$ \displaystyle[M]_{\hbar}(f_{1}(H_{1}),\ldots,f_{n}(H_{n}))=\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}\left(\int_{(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n+1}\to\mathbb{P}^{r}}f_{1}(H_{1})\ldots f_{n}(H_{n})[\mathcal{O}_{\tau^{\leq k+1}(M\oplus\ast)}]\right)\hbar^{k} \displaystyle\in A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})[\hbar]\cong QH^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r}). $$

See Section 4, where we exposit the geometric construction of the small equivariant quantum cohomology of $\mathbb{P}^{r}$ , which parallels the above.

## 3. Statement of Results, extended example, and high level outline

In this section, we state our main results, give an extended example, and give a high level outline of our proofs.

Our first result computes the $GL_{r+1}$ -equivariant Chow class of $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ .

The non-equivariant class $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ computed in [42] (see Theorem 5.2) is an integer point transform of $(r+\frac{1}{n})(1,\ldots,1)-(r+1)P_{M}$ . By Brion’s Theorem [11], it can be written as $f_{M}(H_{1},\ldots,H_{n},H_{1}^{r+1},\ldots,H_{n}^{r+1})$ , where $f_{M}$ is a rational function that does not depend on $r$ . The expression in Theorem 1 is then $f_{M}(H_{1},\ldots,H_{n},F(H_{1}),\ldots,F(H_{n}))$ . We will see later that a similar procedure computes the $GL_{r+1}$ -equivariant class $[\overline{\Gamma_{M}}]$ using the independence polytope $I_{M}$ .

#### Theorem 1 (Theorem 9.1).

Let $M$ be a $d\times n$ matrix with nonzero columns $x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}$ . If ${\rm rk}(M)<d$ , then $\mathcal{O}_{M}=0$ . Otherwise, for each permutation $\sigma\in S_{n}$ , let $B(\sigma)$ be the lexicographically first $d$ -element subset $\{i_{1},\ldots,i_{d}\}\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with respect to the ordering $\sigma(1)\prec\cdots\prec\sigma(n)$ such that $x_{i_{1}},\ldots,x_{i_{d}}$ is a basis of $K^{d}$ . Then for indeterminates $z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}$ , the expression

$$ \sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}}\left(\prod_{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus B(\sigma)}F(z_{i})\right)\frac{1}{(z_{\sigma(2)}-z_{\sigma(1)})\ldots(z_{\sigma(n)}-z_{\sigma(n-1)})} $$

is a polynomial of degree at most $r$ in each $z_{i}$ with coefficients in $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}({\rm pt})$ , and the equivariant Chow class $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ is given by evaluating this polynomial at $H_{1},\ldots,H_{n}$ .

The above formula, and the one we describe later for $[\overline{\Gamma_{M}}]$ , also provide formulas for $GL_{r+1}\times(K^{\times})^{n}$ -equivariant classes of the analogues of $\mathcal{O}_{M}$ and $\overline{\Gamma_{M}}$ in $\mathbb{A}^{(r+1)\times n}$ (see Section 13). In particular, this recovers the torus-equivariant classes of torus orbits in the Grassmannian.

Because of the connections to sums over lattice points of rescaled rank and independence polytopes, the formulas for $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ and for $[\overline{\Gamma_{M}}]$ turn out to be additive and valuative respectively.

#### Theorem 2 (Theorem 7.1, Corollary 11.3).

For fixed $\mathbb{P}^{r}$ , the maps $M\mapsto[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ and $M\mapsto[\overline{\Gamma_{M}}]$ from $d\times n$ matrices to equivariant Chow classes are additive and valuative associations respectively. In particular, $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ and $[\overline{\Gamma_{M}}]$ only depend on the matroid of $M$ .

The classes $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ also behave well under series and parallel connection.

#### Theorem 3 (Theorem 8.1).

For $i\in\{1,2\}$ let $M_{i}$ be a $d_{i}\times n_{i}$ matrix. Taking series and parallel connections along the last column of $M_{1}$ and the first column of $M_{2}$ , we have in $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{\otimes n_{1}-1}\otimes QH^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})\otimes A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{\otimes n_{2}-1}\cong A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{\otimes n_{1}+n_{2}-1}[\hbar]$ the equality

$$ [\mathcal{O}_{M_{1}}]\star[\mathcal{O}_{M_{2}}]=[\mathcal{O}_{P(M_{1},M_{2})}]+\hbar[\mathcal{O}_{S(M_{1},M_{2})}] $$

where the quantum product $\star$ is taken along the last factor of $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}((\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n_{1}})=A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{\otimes n_{1}}$ and the first factor of $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}((\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n_{2}})=A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{\otimes n_{2}}$ .

The next theorem develops the key properties of the operations $[M]_{\hbar}$ .

#### Theorem 4 (Section 10).

Fix $r\geq 0$ . Then the $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}({\rm pt})$ -linear operations

$$ [M]_{\hbar}:A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{\otimes n}\to QH^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r}) $$

satisfy

$$ [z^{r}][F(z)^{k}][M_{\hbar}]=[\mathcal{O}_{\tau^{\leq(k+1)}M}]^{\dagger}. $$

The following properties uniquely characterize the $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}({\rm pt})$ -linear operations $[M]_{\hbar}$ .

- (1) Let $\ast$ denote the $1\times 1$ identity matrix. Then

$$ [\ast]_{\hbar}(f(H))=\overline{f}(z). $$

- (2) If $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ are matrices with $n_{1}$ and $n_{2}$ columns respectively, then

$$ [M_{1}\oplus M_{2}]_{\hbar}=[M_{1}]_{\hbar}\star[M_{2}]_{\hbar}, $$

where $[M_{1}]_{\hbar}$ applies to the first $n_{1}$ tensor factors and $[M_{2}]_{\hbar}$ applies to the last $n_{2}$ tensor factors.

- (3) If $M$ is a $d\times n$ matrix and $\tau^{\leq k}$ is a general $k\times d$ matrix, then $[\tau^{\leq k}M]_{\hbar}$ is the reduction of $[M]_{\hbar}$ modulo $\hbar^{k}=F(z)^{k}$ .

- (4) The association $M\mapsto[M]_{\hbar}$ is valuative. For fixed $n$ and possibly varying $d$ , the operation $[M]_{\hbar}$ depends only on the matroid of $M$ .

- (5) The actions of the symmetric group $S_{n}$ on the columns of $M$ and on $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{\otimes n}$ are compatible.

The next theorem relates the class $[\overline{\Gamma_{M}}]$ to the operation $[M]_{\hbar}$ . Recall that $\mu_{M}^{*}:A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}((\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n})\to A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{(r+1)\times d-1})$ was defined via convolution with $[\overline{\Gamma_{M}}]$ .

#### Theorem 5 (Theorem 11.1).

Define

$$ \displaystyle q \displaystyle:QH^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})\to A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{(r+1)\times d-1})\text{ by }z\mapsto H \displaystyle\ell \displaystyle:A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{(r+1)\times d-1})\to QH^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})\text{ by }\ell(f(H))=\widetilde{f}(z), $$

where $\widetilde{f}$ is the reduction of $f$ modulo $F(H)^{d}$ (analogously to Definition 2.6). Then

$$ \mu_{M}^{*}=q\circ[M]_{\hbar},\qquad[M]_{\hbar}=\ell\circ\mu_{M}^{*}. $$

#### Remark 3.1.

From this, we can express the $GL_{r+1}$ -equivariant class $[\overline{\Gamma_{M}}]$ in terms of the classes $[\mathcal{O}_{\tau^{\leq k+1}(M\oplus\ast)}]$ used to define $[M]_{\hbar}$ (see Theorem 11.1). This expression in turn may be seen as an application of Brion’s formula applied to $(r+\frac{1}{n})(1,\ldots,1)-(r+1)I_{M}$ with $H$ used non-equivariantly as a grading variable to ensure the expression is homogenous of rank $rn$ , see the proof of Theorem 10.3.

We give an application to enumerative geometry. Given a smooth quintic plane curve $X\subset\mathbb{P}^{2}$ , there is a rational map

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{X}:(\mathbb{P}^{2})^{\vee}\dashrightarrow\overline{\mathcal{M}_{0,5}}/S_{5} $$

sending a line $\ell$ to the moduli of the intersection $\ell\cap X$ as a quintuple of points on $\ell\cong\mathbb{P}^{1}$ . Cadman and Laza [13] showed that if every line intersects $X$ in at least three points, then

$$ \displaystyle\deg(\phi_{X})=2\cdot(\text{\# bitangents of $X$})+4\cdot(\text{\# flexes of $X$})=2\cdot 120+4\cdot 45=420. $$

We extend this to hypersurfaces $X\subset\mathbb{P}^{r}$ of degree $d=2r+1$ for all $r$ by computing $\deg(\phi_{X})$ and separately expressing $\deg(\phi_{X})$ in terms of the lines tri-incident to $X$ .

#### Theorem 6 (Theorem 12.5).

Let $X\subset\mathbb{P}^{r}$ be a hypersurface of degree $d=2r+1$ such that every line meets $X$ in at least three points and is not contained in $X$ . The degree of

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{X}:\mathbb{G}(1,r)\dashrightarrow\overline{\mathcal{M}_{0,d}}/S_{d} $$

is the difference between the coefficients of $u^{r-1}v^{r-1}$ and $u^{r-2}v^{r}$ in the expansion of

$$ \displaystyle d(d-1)(d-2)\prod_{k=2}^{d-2}(ku+(d-k)v). $$

In fact Theorem 12.5 computes the class of a general fiber of $\phi_{X}$ when we drop the assumption $d=2r+1$ . Finally, we can express $\deg(\phi_{X})$ in terms of numbers of tri-incident lines.

#### Theorem 7 (Theorem 12.7).

Let $X\subset\mathbb{P}^{r}$ be a hypersurface of degree $d=2r+1$ such that every line meets $X$ in at least three points and is not contained in $X$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\deg(\phi_{X})=\sum_{a\geq b>1,a+b+1=d}{2n_{a,b,1}}+4n_{d-2,1,1}, $$

where $n_{a,b,c}$ is the number (counted with certain multiplicities) of lines that intersect $X$ at three points with multiplicities exactly $a,b,c$ .

We will see later that Theorem 7 is induced by a relation between generalized matrix orbit classes arising from Theorem 2.

### 3.1. Extended Example

In this subsection we present an extended example to demonstrate the key aspects of our results.

#### 3.1.1. Setup

Let $p_{1},\ldots,p_{6}\in\mathbb{P}^{2}$ be the points depicted below (or any other six points with the same collinearity relations).

Let $A$ be any $3\times 6$ matrix whose projectivized columns are $p_{1},\ldots,p_{6}$ . For any $r\geq 2$ , the cycle $[\mathcal{O}_{A}]\in A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}((\mathbb{P}^{r})^{6})$ is the closure of the $GL_{r+1}$ -orbit of $(p_{1},\ldots,p_{6})\in(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{6}$ , where each point $p_{i}$ is considered as an element of $\mathbb{P}^{r}$ via any linear inclusion $\mathbb{P}^{2}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{r}$ (Proposition 2.2).

#### 3.1.2. Formula for $[\mathcal{O}_{A}]$

The rank polytope of (the column matroid of) $A$ is the convex hull of the 17 points

$$ \displaystyle\{e_{i}+e_{j}+e_{k}\mid p_{i},p_{j},p_{k}\text{ span }\mathbb{P}^{2}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{6}. $$

and Theorem 1 expresses the class $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]\in A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}((\mathbb{P}^{r})^{6})$ as a sum of $6!$ rational functions. However, such a large sum is difficult to manipulate in practice. Instead, we may understand $[\mathcal{O}_{A}]$ by computing the Kronecker dual

$$ [\mathcal{O}_{A}]^{\dagger}:A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{\otimes 6}\to A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}({\rm pt}), $$

which we recall is defined by

$$ [\mathcal{O}_{A}]^{\dagger}(f_{1}(H),\ldots,f_{6}(H))=\int_{(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{6}}[\mathcal{O}_{A}]f_{1}(H_{1})\ldots f_{6}(H_{6}) $$

for any polynomials $f_{1},\ldots,f_{6}$ with coefficients in $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}({\rm pt})$ .

#### 3.1.3. Degenerations

In many cases (such as this one), we can compute Kronecker dual classes efficiently by breaking the problem into smaller pieces.

We can relate $[\mathcal{O}_{A}]$ with other classes through the following degeneration tree. Here $B,C,D,E$ are $3\times 6$ matrices whose projectivized columns are the depicted point configurations.

The rank polytopes of $A$ , $B$ , $C$ , $D$ , and $E$ are related by subdivisions. The hyperplane $\{x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{4}=2\}$ separates the rank polytope $P_{B}$ of $B$ into the rank polytopes $P_{A}$ and $P_{C}$ of $A$ and $C$ respectively. Similarly, the hyperplane $\{x_{1}+x_{3}+x_{6}=2\}$ separates $P_{D}$ into $P_{B}$ and $P_{E}$ .

Accordingly, the cycle $\mathcal{O}_{B}$ degenerates to a union $\mathcal{O}_{A}\cup\mathcal{O}_{C}$ and $\mathcal{O}_{D}$ degenerates to a union $\mathcal{O}_{B}\cup\mathcal{O}_{E}$ (Theorem 6.2), so we get

$$ \displaystyle[\mathcal{O}_{B}]=[\mathcal{O}_{A}]+[\mathcal{O}_{C}]\qquad[\mathcal{O}_{D}]=[\mathcal{O}_{B}]+[\mathcal{O}_{E}]. $$

Not all subdivisions of rank polytopes yield degenerations of the cycles $\mathcal{O}_{M}$ , but they all yield relations between the generalized matrix orbit classes $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ (Theorem 2).

Therefore,

$$ [\mathcal{O}_{A}]=[\mathcal{O}_{D}]-[\mathcal{O}_{C}]-[\mathcal{O}_{E}] $$

so

$$ [\mathcal{O}_{A}]^{\dagger}=[\mathcal{O}_{D}]^{\dagger}-[\mathcal{O}_{C}]^{\dagger}-[\mathcal{O}_{E}]^{\dagger}. $$

#### 3.1.4. Kronecker duals to Schubert Matroids

To compute $[\mathcal{O}_{A}]^{\dagger}$ , it remains to compute $[\mathcal{O}_{C}]^{\dagger}$ , $[\mathcal{O}_{D}]^{\dagger}$ , and $[\mathcal{O}_{E}]^{\dagger}$ , for which we will use the operations

$$ [C]_{\hbar},[D]_{\hbar},[E]_{\hbar}:A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{\otimes 6}\to QH^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})=A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}({\rm pt})[z][\hbar]/(\hbar-F(z)). $$

(Theorem 4).

To compute $[C]_{\hbar},[D]_{\hbar},[E]_{\hbar}$ , we will use the fact that the column matroids of $C$ , $D$ , $E$ are Schubert matroids. For example, we may write

$$ D=\operatorname{Sch}(2,3,\{4,5,6\},\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}). $$

Hence, by the definition of a Schubert matroid and Theorem 4 we have

$$ \displaystyle[D]_{\hbar}(f_{1}(H),\ldots,f_{6}(H)) \displaystyle=f_{1}(z)f_{2}(z)f_{3}(z)(f_{4}(z)f_{5}(z)f_{6}(z)\text{ mod }F(z)^{2})\text{ mod }F(z)^{3} $$

for any polynomials $f_{1},\ldots,f_{6}$ of degree at most $r$ with coefficients in $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}({\rm pt})$ . We have thus expressed $[D]_{\hbar}$ using polynomial multiplication and division with remainder.

By Theorem 4 again, we have

$$ \displaystyle[\mathcal{O}_{D}]^{\dagger}(f_{1}(H),\ldots,f_{6}(H)) \displaystyle=[z^{r}][F(z)^{2}][D]_{\hbar}(f_{1}(H),\ldots,f_{6}(H)) \displaystyle=[z^{r}][F(z)^{2}](f_{1}(z)f_{2}(z)f_{3}(z)(f_{4}(z)f_{5}(z)f_{6}(z)\text{ mod }F(z)^{2})). $$

We can perform a similar procedure for the matrices $C$ and $E$ , yielding

$$ \displaystyle[\mathcal{O}_{C}]^{\dagger}(f_{1}(H),\ldots,f_{6}(H)) \displaystyle=[z^{r}][F(z)^{2}][C]_{\hbar}(f_{1}(H),\ldots,f_{6}(H)) \displaystyle=[z^{r}][F(z)^{2}](f_{1}(z)f_{2}(z)f_{4}(z)(f_{3}(z)f_{5}(z)f_{6}(z)\text{ mod }F(z))) \displaystyle[\mathcal{O}_{E}]^{\dagger}(f_{1}(H),\ldots,f_{6}(H)) \displaystyle=[z^{r}][F(z)^{2}][E]_{\hbar}(f_{1}(H),\ldots,f_{6}(H)) \displaystyle=[z^{r}][F(z)^{2}](f_{1}(z)f_{3}(z)f_{6}(z)(f_{2}(z)f_{4}(z)f_{5}(z)\text{ mod }F(z))). $$

Hence $[\mathcal{O}_{A}]^{\dagger}$ is given by

$$ \displaystyle[\mathcal{O}_{A}]^{\dagger}(f_{1}(H),\ldots,f_{6}(H))=[z^{r}][F(z)^{2}]( \displaystyle f_{1}(z)f_{2}(z)f_{3}(z)(f_{4}(z)f_{5}(z)f_{6}(z)\text{ mod }F(z)^{2}) \displaystyle-f_{1}(z)f_{2}(z)f_{4}(z)(f_{3}(z)f_{5}(z)f_{6}(z)\text{ mod }F(z)) \displaystyle-f_{1}(z)f_{3}(z)f_{6}(z)(f_{2}(z)f_{4}(z)f_{5}(z)\text{ mod }F(z))). $$

for all polynomials $f_{1},\ldots,f_{6}$ of degree at most $r$ with coefficients in $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}({\rm pt})$ . We will see in Section 10.4 how to apply a similar procedure to compute $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]^{\dagger}$ for all $M$ .

### 3.2. High level outline

We now give a high level outline of our proofs. A flow chart containing the logical structure of the proofs is given in Figure 1. Input from the literature is shown in dotted boxes, while our contributions are in solid boxes.

*Figure 1. Logical structure of proofs*

#### 3.2.1. Non-equivariant additivity

In Theorem 5.2, we show the non-equivariant additivity of $M\mapsto[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ . Li’s result [42] exhibits the non-equivariant class $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ as the sum of monomials in the $H_{i}$ variables whose exponent sequence lies inside the region $(r+\frac{1}{n})(1,\ldots,1)-(r+1)P_{M}$ , so the result essentially follows by definition.

#### 3.2.2. Equivariant degenerations of orbits

In Theorem 6.2, we show that any flat limit of the form $\mathcal{O}_{M(t)}$ as $t\to 0$ has the property that the special fiber is $\bigcup_{i=1}^{k}[\mathcal{O}_{M_{i}}]$ for some matrices $M_{i}$ such that the rank polytopes subdivide $P_{M_{p}}$ for $p$ general. In particular, we deduce in Corollary 6.3 additivity relations of the form

$$ [\mathcal{O}_{M(p)}]=\sum_{i=1}^{k}[\mathcal{O}_{M_{i}}] $$

arising from such degenerations. We do this by identifying enough $\mathcal{O}_{M_{i}}$ in the limit so that both sides agree non-equivariantly, and then conclude by the fact that an effective cycle that is non-equivariantly zero is also equivariantly zero. Note at this point we do not know that $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ depends only on the matroid of $M$ .

#### 3.2.3. Relations generated by degenerations

Even though Theorem 6.2 provides many relations among the classes $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ , it is not clear that these relations induced from degenerations imply additivity of $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ . We will show that they in fact do.

We prove in Lemma 7.2 that for $M$ having a particular type of matroid polytope, which we call a “cone-like matroid polytope” (see Definition 7.3), $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ depends only on the matroid of $M$ . Given $M,M^{\prime}$ with the same cone-like matroid polytope, we do this by creating a flat degeneration with two special fibers $\mathcal{O}_{M}$ and $\mathcal{O}_{M^{\prime}}$ .

Using degenerations to reduce to a certain class of matrices with “positive cone-like matroid polytopes”, which satisfy no non-trivial additive relations, is a delicate combinatorial argument which modifies the algorithm from [16, Appendix A]. The essential point is that we closely follow a sequence of infinite polytope subdivisions, which when restricted to $\Delta_{d,n}$ yield a sequence of finite polytope subdivisions. This is done by attaching a certain cone to each matrix in our sequence of degenerations, which governs future degenerations based on past ones. We defer the more detailed high level explanation to Section 7.1.

#### 3.2.4. Series and parallel connection

We show that parallel and series connection are given by certain convolutions with the classes of the diagonal in $(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{3}$ and the class of collinear triples of points in $(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{3}$ respectively in Section 8. Then identical to the standard derivation of the equivariant $3$ -point Gromov-witten invariants of $\mathbb{P}^{r}$ , we are able to deduce Theorem 3.

#### 3.2.5. Series-parallel matroids

To analyze series-parallel matrices, through their recursive definition it suffices to have a good understanding of how the $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ classes behave under series and parallel connections of the underlying matrices.

Through a clever application of partial fraction decomposition combined with Theorem 3, we are able to show that for each series-parallel matroid there is a universal rational function in $2n$ variables such that for any $r$ , if we substitute $H_{1},\ldots,H_{n},F(H_{1}),\ldots,F(H_{n})$ into the variables then we formally recover the equivariant class. Note that as $r$ increases, the polynomial $F(H_{i})$ changes with the addition of more $t_{i}$ variables.

#### 3.2.6. Formula for $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ (Theorem 1)

Once we have additivity of the classes $M\mapsto[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ , to prove Theorem 1 it suffices to prove it for a special class of matrices whose matroid polytopes generate all others through additivity relations. [16] used the additive basis of Schubert matroids, which we will analyze in detail later, but we instead use series-parallel matroids, as every Schubert matroid polytope can be subdivided into series-parallel matroid polytopes.

From additivity we are able to deduce the existence of a rational function for any matrix $M$ determining $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ as above. We show in Theorem 8.2 that this rational function is uniquely determined by its values when substituting $H_{1},\ldots,H_{n},H_{1}^{r+1},\ldots,H_{n}^{r+1}$ (giving the nonequivariant class of $\mathcal{O}_{M}$ ), so it must agree with the rational function produced by Brion’s formula for the non-equivariant classes. Theorem 1 then follows by substituting $F(H_{i})$ in place of $H_{i}^{r+1}$ in the formula, which is done in Section 9.

#### 3.2.7. Properties of $[M]_{\hbar}$ (Theorem 4)

To prove Theorem 4, we use an analogous non-equivariant for every $r$ to equivariant strategy as above, and show that non-equivariantly the data of $[M]_{\hbar}$ can be encoded via a sum of monomials inside $(r+\frac{1}{n})(1,1,\ldots,1)-(r+1)I_{M}$ , by slicing the independence polytope according to the hyperplanes $\{\sum x_{i}=k\}$ with $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ , and showing that each slice, homogenized with an extra variable $H_{n+1}$ , appears as the rank polytope of $\tau^{\leq k+1}(M\oplus\ast)$ . Then all of the parts of Theorem 4 readily follows as shown in Section 10. For example valuativity of $[M]_{\hbar}$ follows from the fact that valuativity can be interpreted in terms of independence polytopes, and $[M\oplus N]_{\hbar}=[M]_{\hbar}\star[N]_{\hbar}$ follows from the fact that $I_{M\oplus N}=I_{M}\times I_{N}$ .

#### 3.2.8. Convolution with graph closure $\overline{\Gamma_{M}}$ (Theorem 5)

Finally, Theorem 5 follows from carefully analyzing the wonderful compactification of [41], where we have to relate the images of classes under $(\mu_{M})_{*}$ , and $(\mu_{\tau^{\leq k+1}(M\oplus\ast)})_{*}$ under various pullbacks and pushforwards. Then valuativity of $[\overline{\Gamma_{M}}]$ from Theorem 2 follows from the corresponding valuativity of $[M]_{\hbar}$ . This is done in Section 11.

## 4. Motivating example and the connection of $\mu_{M}$ with $QH_{GL_{r+1}}^{\bullet}(\mathbb{P}^{r})$

Here we make precise the connection between generalized matrix orbits and the small equivariant quantum cohomology of $\mathbb{P}^{r}$ , assuming the part of Theorem 2 asserting that $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ depends only on the matroid of $M$ . In this section only, we will assume $\operatorname{char}K=0$ .

The concrete focus of this section will be on the following problem.

#### Problem 4.1.

What is the class in $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}((\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n})$ of the closure of the $GL_{r+1}$ -orbit of $(p_{1},\ldots,p_{n})\in(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n}$ , where $p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}\in\mathbb{P}^{r}$ are general? 11 1 The expression for the class of this orbit closure computed in [9, Theorem 5.1] is incorrect because their expression for “ $[Y_{\pi(v)}]_{T}$ ” does not satisfy the degree hypothesis of [9, Theorem 3.5 (ii)].

Let $M_{r+1}$ be an $(r+1)\times n$ matrix whose projectivized columns are these general $p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}$ . By Proposition 2.2 the $GL_{r+1}$ -orbit closure of $(p_{1},\ldots,p_{n})$ is $\mathcal{O}_{M}$ if $n>r+1$ and $(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n}$ if $n\leq r+1$ .

In this section we will answer the following more refined problem, which yields orbit closures for $d+1\leq r+1$ , generalized matrix orbits for $r+1<d+1<n$ , and $0$ for $n\leq d+1$ .

#### Problem 4.2.

If $M_{d+1}$ is a general $(d+1)\times n$ matrix, what is $[\mathcal{O}_{M_{d+1}}]\in A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}((\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n})$ ?

We will assume $n\geq d+2$ for the remainder of Section 4.

### 4.1. Specialization

We first reduce Problem 4.2 to a fact about the small equivariant quantum cohomology of $\mathbb{P}^{r}$ . Let $p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}$ be the projectivized columns of $M_{d+1}$ .

We will show in Theorem 7.1 that the class $[\mathcal{O}_{M_{d+1}}]$ depends only on the matroid of $p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}$ . Hence, rather than choosing $p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}$ to be general, we may choose them in any way such that any $d+1$ of them are linearly independent.

Therefore, we can choose $p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}$ to be distinct points on a rational normal curve $C\subset\mathbb{P}^{d}$ . In this way, we may view $C$ as an $n$ -pointed rational curve $(\mathbb{P}^{1},p_{1},\ldots,p_{n})$ . We will now show that $\mathcal{O}_{M_{d+1}}$ is the closure of

$$ \{(\psi(p_{1}),\ldots,\psi(p_{n}))\mid\text{$\psi:\mathbb{P}^{1}\to\mathbb{P}^{r}$ is a degree $d$ map}\}. $$

Afterwards, we may break our problem into smaller parts by using the structure of $\overline{{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n}}$ , the coarse moduli space of $n$ -pointed stable curves of genus $0$ .

### 4.2. Small Equivariant Quantum Cohomology of $\mathbb{P}^{r}$

At this point it makes sense to recall small equivariant quantum cohomology [30], specifically in the case of $\mathbb{P}^{r}$ . We will use the Kontsevich space, the coarse moduli space $\overline{{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n}}(\mathbb{P}^{r},d)$ whose points are $(\mathcal{C},\psi)$ where $\mathcal{C}$ is a genus $0$ curve with $n$ marked points $p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}$ and $\psi:\mathcal{C}\to\mathbb{P}^{r}$ is a degree $d$ stable map. There is a map $\pi:\overline{\mathcal{M}_{0,n}}(\mathbb{P}^{r},d)\to\overline{\mathcal{M}_{0,n}}$ that forgets the morphism to $\mathbb{P}^{r}$ and stabilizes the domain curve and there are evaluation maps ${\rm ev}_{1},\ldots,{\rm ev}_{n}:\overline{\mathcal{M}_{0,n}}(\mathbb{P}^{r},d)\to\mathbb{P}^{r}$ that send $(\mathcal{C},\psi)$ to $\psi(p_{1}),\ldots,\psi(p_{n})$ respectively. We thus have the following diagram.

Let $X\subset\overline{{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n}}(\mathbb{P}^{r},d)$ be a $GL_{r+1}$ -equivariant cycle. The convolution operation $\operatorname{conv}_{X,d}:A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}((\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n-1})\to A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})$ is defined by

$$ {\operatorname{conv}}_{X,d}(x)=({\rm ev}_{n})_{*}([X]\cap({\rm ev}_{1},\ldots,{\rm ev}_{n-1})^{*}x). $$

The $\star$ -product of small equivariant quantum cohomology allows one to compute the operation ${\operatorname{conv}}_{\pi^{-1}(\mathcal{C}),d}$ for $\mathcal{C}\in\overline{{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n}}$ , which can be geometrically interpreted as follows. Given effective cycles $X_{1},\ldots,X_{n-1}$ in the projectivization of the universal rank $r+1$ vector bundle, the convolution ${\operatorname{conv}}_{\pi^{-1}(\mathcal{C}),d}([X_{1}]\otimes\ldots\otimes[X_{n-1}])$ should be thought of as the Chow class of the cycle swept out by $\psi(p_{n})$ as $\psi:\mathcal{C}\to\mathbb{P}^{r}$ ranges over all degree $d$ rational maps to fibers of the bundle such that $\psi(p_{i})\in X_{i}$ for $1\leq i\leq n-1$ .

As $\pi$ is flat [40, Remark 2.6.8], ${\operatorname{conv}}_{\pi^{-1}(\mathcal{C}),d}$ is independent of the choice of $\mathcal{C}$ . More generally, the operation ${\operatorname{conv}}_{X,d}$ , where $X$ is an irreducible component of $\pi^{-1}(\mathcal{C})$ , can also be computed using small equivariant quantum cohomology, and if $\pi^{-1}(\mathcal{C})$ has irreducible components $X_{1},\ldots,X_{k}$ , then $\sum_{i=1}^{k}{\operatorname{conv}}_{X_{i},d}={\operatorname{conv}}_{\pi^{-1}(\mathcal{C}),d}$ . The fact that the components of $\pi^{-1}(\mathcal{C})$ have multiplicity one can be deduced either from the deformation theory techniques of [21, Section 5] or from the description in [29, Section 4.1].

In Section 4.5, we will see how for a fixed $\mathcal{C}$ the data of ${\operatorname{conv}}_{\pi^{-1}(\mathcal{C}),d}$ for varying $d$ is encoded in the $\star$ -product on $QH^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})$ .

### 4.3. Connecting the Kontsevich mapping space with $\mu_{M}$

The operation ${\operatorname{conv}}_{X}$ is Kronecker dual (in the first $n-1$ factors of $\mathbb{P}^{r}$ ) to the class

$$ [{\rm ev}_{*}X]\in A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}((\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n})=A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}((\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n-1})\otimes A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r}). $$

We now make a fundamental observation, apparently new in this level of generality. If $X$ is an irreducible component of a fiber $\pi^{-1}(\mathcal{C})$ of $\pi$ , then ${\rm ev}_{*}X$ can be expressed as $\mathcal{O}_{M}$ for an explicit $d\times n$ matrix $M$ , which we show in Lemma 4.3. In the case $d=r+1$ , this is reflected in the fact that $\overline{{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n}}$ embeds into the Chow quotient $(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n}//_{Ch}SL_{r+1}$ [29, Section 3.2].

#### Lemma 4.3.

Let $Z\subset\overline{{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n}}(\mathbb{P}^{r},d)$ be a component of a fiber $\pi^{-1}(\mathcal{C})$ . Then ${\rm ev}_{*}Z=\mathcal{O}_{M}$ for some $(d+1)\times n$ matrix $M$ .

#### Proof.

Suppose that $\mathcal{C}=[(C,p_{1},\ldots,p_{n})]$ and let $C_{1},\ldots,C_{k}$ be the components of $C$ . As one might expect [29, Section 4.1], there is an open locus $Z^{\circ}\subset Z$ and integers $d_{1},\ldots,d_{k}$ such that $Z^{\circ}$ parameterizes maps $C\to\mathbb{P}^{r}$ that restrict to degree $d_{i}$ on each $C_{i}$ .

Let $L$ be the line bundle on $C$ that restricts to $\mathscr{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{1}}(d_{v})$ on each component $C_{v}\cong\mathbb{P}^{1}$ and let $V=H^{0}(C,L)$ . Then $\dim(V)=d+1$ and we have a map $f:C\to\mathbb{P}(V^{\vee})$ .

Let $W=K^{r+1}$ . Each rational map $C\to\mathbb{P}^{r}=\mathbb{P}(W^{\vee})$ that restricts to degree $d_{v}$ on each component $C_{v}$ can be written uniquely as a composition $C\xrightarrow{f}\mathbb{P}(V^{\vee})\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}(W^{\vee})$ , where the map $\mathbb{P}(V^{\vee})\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}(W^{\vee})$ is induced by a linear map $W\to V$ . This is a regular map if and only if the linear system $W\to V=H^{0}(C,L)$ is basepoint-free.

Let $U\subset\mathbb{P}({\rm Hom}(W,V))$ be the open locus of basepoint-free linear systems $W\to V\cong H^{0}(C,L)$ . Then $U$ is nonempty and by the above it embeds into $Z^{\circ}$ . We have a diagram

So $\mathbb{P}({\rm Hom}(W,V))$ and $Z$ share the open set $U$ , and the bottom map is $\mu_{M}$ where $M$ is any matrix with projectivized columns $f(p_{1}),\ldots,f(p_{n})\in\mathbb{P}(V^{\vee})$ . The result now follows. ∎

### 4.4. Degenerating the domain curve

By the proof of Lemma 4.3, we have $\mathcal{O}_{M_{d+1}}={\rm ev}_{*}\pi^{-1}(\mathcal{C})$ if $\mathcal{C}=[(\mathbb{P}^{1},p_{1},\ldots,p_{n})]$ , where $p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}\in\mathbb{P}^{1}$ have the same moduli as in Section 4.1. Since $\pi$ is flat, the same equation holds for any $\mathcal{C}$ , so we can choose $\mathcal{C}=[(C_{0},p_{1},\ldots,p_{n})]$ to be a chain of $n-2$ rational curves.

Let $\Gamma_{0}$ be the dual graph of $C_{0}$ , which is a chain of $n-2$ vertices connected by edges. Then the fiber of $\pi$ over $(C_{0},p_{1},\ldots,p_{n})$ has $\binom{n-3+d}{d}$ components, indexed by assignments of degrees to the $n-2$ vertices of $\Gamma_{0}$ that sum to $d$ . However, most components push forward to zero under ${\rm ev}_{*}$ for dimension reasons, and only $\binom{n-2}{d}$ components, corresponding to assignments of degrees of 0’s and 1’s, survive.

Therefore, the cycle $\mathcal{O}_{M_{d+1}}$ degenerates to $\binom{n-2}{d}$ generalized matrix orbits by Lemma 4.3.

denotes the convolution ${\operatorname{conv}}_{Z_{i,j},i+j}(f,g,h)$ , where $Z_{i,j}\subset\overline{{\mathcal{M}}_{0,4}}(\mathbb{P}^{r},i+j)$ is defined as follows. Let $\mathcal{C}=[(C,p_{1},p_{2},p_{3},p_{4})]$ , where $C=C_{1}\cup C_{2}$ be the reducible curve in $\overline{{\mathcal{M}}_{0,4}}$ with $p_{1},p_{2}\in C_{1}$ and $p_{3},p_{4}\in C_{2}$ . Then $Z_{i,j}$ is the component of the fiber of $\pi^{-1}(\mathcal{C})$ generically parameterizing maps $C\to\mathbb{P}^{r}$ that restrict to degree $i$ on $C_{1}$ and degree $j$ on $C_{2}$ .

Here, we are using the fact that the composition of convolution operations corresponds to the gluing morphism between Kontsevich spaces, so that

$$ \displaystyle{\operatorname{conv}}_{Z_{i,j},i+j}(f,g,h)={\operatorname{conv}}_{\pi^{-1}({\rm pt}),j}({\operatorname{conv}}_{\pi^{-1}({\rm pt}),i}(f,g),h). $$

There are no issues with multiplicities because the gluing morphism will always be an isomorphism in our case [21, Lemma 12 (i)].
