as the $Z_{i,j}$ for $i+j=d$ are exactly the components of the fiber $\pi^{-1}(\mathcal{C})$ . By the flatness of $\pi$ , the class of $\pi^{-1}(\mathcal{C})$ is unchanged if we redistribute the points $p_{1},\ldots,p_{4}$ , implying $(f\star g)\star h$ does not depend on the ordering of $f$ , $g$ , and $h$ , so $\star$ is commutative and associative.

In turn, the discussion in Section 4.4 shows that (taking $(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{4}\to\mathbb{P}^{r}$ the last projection)

$$ {\operatorname{conv}}_{\pi^{-1}(\mathcal{C}),d}(f,g,h)=\int_{(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{4}\to\mathbb{P}^{r}}[\mathcal{O}_{M_{d+1}}]f(H_{1})g(H_{2})h(H_{3}), $$

where $M_{d+1}$ is a general $(d+1)\times 4$ matrix. In general, the same reasoning shows

$$ f_{1}\star\cdots\star f_{n-1}=\sum_{d=0}^{n}\hbar^{d}{\operatorname{conv}}_{\pi^{-1}(\mathcal{C}),d}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n-1}) $$

thus deducing the following theorem, which we will use to find $[\mathcal{O}_{M_{d+1}}]$ .

#### Theorem 4.5.

We have

$$ \displaystyle f_{1}\star\cdots\star f_{n-1} \displaystyle=\sum_{d=0}^{n-1}\left(\hbar^{d}\int_{(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n}\to\mathbb{P}^{r}}{[\mathcal{O}_{M_{d+1}}]f_{1}(H_{1})\cdots f_{n-1}(H_{n-1})}\right). $$

#### Remark 4.6.

This holds by Theorem 4 as follows. The equation is equivalently written as

$$ [\ast]_{\hbar}(f_{1})\star[\ast]_{\hbar}(f_{2})\star\ldots\star[\ast]_{\hbar}(f_{n-1})=[I_{n-1}]_{\hbar}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{n-1}), $$

and the two sides are equal again by repeatedly applying Theorem 4. By the simple presentation of $QH^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})$ described in Section 2.3, computing $f_{1}\star\cdots\star f_{n}$ reduces to polynomial multiplication and expansion in terms of powers of the polynomial $F(H)$ .

### 4.6. Computing $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ for a general $d\times n$ matrix

Recall the formulas from Section 2.3. Note that $\int_{\mathbb{P}^{r}}[\hbar]f(H)\star g(H)=[z^{r}][F(z)]\overline{f}(z)\overline{g}(z)=0$ for degree reasons. Applying $\star f_{n}$ to the right of both sides of Theorem 4.5 and applying $\int_{\mathbb{P}^{r}}$ , we deduce that

$$ \int_{(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n}}[\mathcal{O}_{M_{d+1}}]f_{1}(H_{1})\cdots f_{n}(H_{n})=[z^{r}][F(z)^{d}]\overline{f_{1}}(z)\cdots\overline{f_{n}}(z). $$

Note if we assume Theorem 4, then this also follows from

$$ [\mathcal{O}_{M_{d+1}}]^{\dagger}=[\mathcal{O}_{\tau^{\leq d+1}I_{n}}]^{\dagger}=[z^{r}][F(z)^{d}][I_{n}]_{\hbar}. $$

We will use this to construct the formula for $[\mathcal{O}_{M_{d+1}}]$ .

#### Theorem 4.7.

The equivariant Chow class $[\mathcal{O}_{M_{d+1}}]$ is given by

$$ \displaystyle[\mathcal{O}_{M_{d+1}}]=[z^{r}][F(z)^{d}]\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{F(z)-F(H_{i})}{z-H_{i}}. $$

#### Proof.

For any polynomial $f$ with coefficients in $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}({\rm pt})$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{P}^{r}}\frac{F(z)-F(H)}{z-H}f(H) \displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{P}^{r}}\frac{F(z)-F(H)}{z-H}\overline{f}(H) \displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{P}^{r}}\frac{F(z)-F(H)}{z-H}\overline{f}(z)+\int_{\mathbb{P}^{r}}\frac{F(z)-F(H)}{z-H}(\overline{f}(H)-\overline{f}(z)) \displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{P}^{r}}\frac{F(z)-F(H)}{z-H}\overline{f}(z)+\int_{\mathbb{P}^{r}}\frac{\overline{f}(z)-\overline{f}(H)}{z-H}(F(H)-F(z)) \displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{P}^{r}}\frac{F(z)-F(H)}{z-H}\overline{f}(z)+0-0 \displaystyle=\overline{f}(z); $$

that is, $\frac{F(z)-F(H)}{z-H}\in A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})\otimes QH^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})$ is Kronecker dual to the lifting map $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})\to QH^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})$ . Hence

$$ \int_{(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{F(z)-F(H_{i})}{z-H_{i}}f_{i}(H_{i})=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\overline{f_{i}}(z). $$

Applying $[z^{r}][F(z)^{d}]$ to both sides of this equation yields the desired result. ∎

#### Corollary 4.8.

The expression

$$ \sum_{|A|=d+1}\left(\prod_{j\not\in A}F(z_{j})\right)\sum_{i\in A}\prod_{j\neq i}\frac{(-1)^{n-d+1}}{z_{i}-z_{j}} $$

is a polynomial in $z_{1},\ldots,z_{r}$ , and $[\mathcal{O}_{M_{d+1}}]$ is obtained by evaluating this polynomial at $z_{i}=H_{i}$ .

#### Proof.

Apply partial fraction decomposition to the denominator of the expression in Theorem 4.7. This will also follow from the general expression in Theorem 9.1. ∎

## 5. What is known non-equivariantly

In this section we recall from the literature the results on non-equivariant Chow classes associated to generalized matrix orbit maps that we will be extending equivariantly.

Non-equivariantly, there is a good understanding of generalized matrix orbits and more. It has been shown in [42] that we can express the non-equivariant Chow class of the image of $\mu:\mathbb{P}(W)\dashrightarrow\prod\mathbb{P}(W_{i})$ induced by linear maps $\phi_{i}:W\to W_{i}$ in terms of the data of the polymatroid of the subspaces $U_{i}=\phi_{i}^{*}(W_{i}^{\vee})\subseteq W^{\vee}$ , i.e. the data of $\dim(\sum_{i\in A}U_{i})$ for all subsets $A\subseteq[n]$ . To be more precise, consider a resolution of $\mu$ given by the diagram

Then analogously to generalized matrix orbits as in Section 2.4, for a non-equivariant class $\alpha\in A^{\bullet}(\mathbb{P}(W))$ , we define $\mu_{*}(\alpha):=\widetilde{\mu}_{*}\pi^{*}\alpha$ , which is independent of $B$ .

#### Theorem 5.1 ([42, Theorem 1.1]).

Let $\phi_{i}:W\to W_{i}$ be nonzero linear maps, and let $U_{i}=\phi^{*}(W_{i}^{\vee})\subseteq W_{i}^{\vee}$ . Consider the rational map

$$ \mu:\mathbb{P}(W)\dashrightarrow\prod\mathbb{P}(W_{i}). $$

Then we have

$$ \mu_{*}(H^{j})=\sum\prod_{i=1}^{n}H_{i}^{\dim(W_{i})-1-e_{i}} $$

where the sum is over all tuples $(e_{1},\ldots,e_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i\in A}e_{i}<\dim\sum_{i\in A}U_{i}\qquad\text{for all nonempty $A\subseteq[n]$ and} \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}e_{i}=\dim(W)-1-j. $$

Recall that given a $d\times n$ matrix $M$ with no zero columns, we defined the map $\mu_{M}:\mathbb{P}^{(r+1)\times d-1}\dashrightarrow(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n}$ by matrix multiplication $A\mapsto AM$ of $(r+1)\times d$ matrices with $M$ . Letting $W=K^{d}$ and $V=K^{n}$ , the columns of $M$ are elements of $W$ , and hence induce evaluation functionals $W^{\vee}\to K$ . By tensoring with $V$ , we get induced maps $\phi_{i}:V\otimes W^{\vee}\to V$ . The generalized matrix orbit map $\mu_{M}$ is then induced as above by the linear maps $\phi_{i}$ .

From this description of $\phi_{M}$ , the following follows immediately from Theorem 5.1. Equivariant generalizations are proved in Sections 9 and 11.

#### Theorem 5.2.

Let $M$ be a $d\times n$ matrix. Then the non-equivariant class $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ is given by

$$ [\mathcal{O}_{M}]=\sum\prod_{i=1}^{n}H_{i}^{r-e_{i}} $$

where the sum is over all tuples $(e_{1},\ldots,e_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i\in A}e_{i}<(r+1){\rm rk}(A)\qquad\text{for all nonempty $A\subset[n]$ and} \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}e_{i}=(r+1)d-1. 0<\epsilon_{1},\ldots,\epsilon_{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\epsilon_{i}=1 (e_{1},\ldots,e_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n} \displaystyle(e_{1}+\epsilon_{1},\ldots,e_{n}+\epsilon_{n})\in(r+1)P_{M}. $$

#### Theorem 5.3.

Let $M$ be a $d\times n$ matrix. Then the non-equivariant class of the graph closure $[\overline{\Gamma_{M}}]\in A^{\bullet}(\mathbb{P}^{(r+1)\times d-1}\times(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n})$ of $\mu_{M}$ is given by

$$ [\overline{\Gamma_{M}}]=\sum H^{\sum e_{i}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}H_{i}^{r-e_{i}} $$

where the sum is over all tuples $(e_{1},\ldots,e_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i\in A}e_{i}<(r+1){\rm rk}(A)\qquad\text{for all nonempty $A\subset[n]$.} 0<\epsilon_{1},\ldots,\epsilon_{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\epsilon_{i}\leq 1 (e_{1},\ldots,e_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n} \displaystyle(e_{1}+\epsilon_{1},\ldots,e_{n}+\epsilon_{n})\in(r+1)I_{M}. $$

We note the following immediate corollary of Theorem 5.2.

#### Corollary 5.4.

The non-equivariant class $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ depends only on the matroid of $M$ .

## 6. One-parameter degenerations of generalized matrix orbits

In this section, describe how the cycles $\mathcal{O}_{M}$ degenerate. As a consequence, we obtain relations between the equivariant Chow classes $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ which will be necessary for their later computation.

Degenerations of toric varieties are governed by polytopal geometry, and in particular “regular subdivisions” of their moment polytopes [31, 32]. In particular, Kapranov [35] studied the Chow quotient ${\operatorname{Gr}}(r+1,n)//(K^{\times})^{n}$ and limits of torus orbits in the Grassmannian using polytope subdivisions via the Plücker embedding. Using his isomorphism of Chow quotients ${\operatorname{Gr}}(r+1,n)//(K^{\times})^{n}\cong(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n}//GL_{r+1}$ , general orbits under degeneration split up into certain “sibling orbits” in the special fiber. Speyer investigated this combinatorially [47, 48], developing a notion of tropical linear space to study these degenerations.

We adopt the following conventions.

- (1) Let $D$ be a smooth, affine, finite-type $K$ -scheme of dimension 1 (we will only use the case that $D\subset\mathbb{A}^{1}$ is an open set).

- (2) Let $0\in D$ be a closed point and let $t$ be a uniformizing parameter around 0. By replacing $D$ with a suitable open subset, we may assume that $t$ is regular and vanishes only at $0$ .

- (3) Let $M_{D}:D\to\mathbb{A}^{d\times n}$ be a morphism from $D$ to the space of matrices that maps the generic point to a rank $d$ matrix with no identically zero column.

- (4) Let $P$ be the rank polytope corresponding to the image of the generic point of $D$ under $M_{D}$ . Equivalently, it is the rank polytope of $M_{D}$ evaluated at a general point.

The generalized matrix orbits $\mathcal{O}_{M_{D}(p)}\subset(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n}$ form a flat family over some open subset $U\subset D\setminus\{0\}$ . We are interested in extending this family to a flat family of subvarieties of $(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n}$ over $U\cup\{0\}$ . In other words, we are interested in the flat limit of the generalized matrix orbits $\mathcal{O}_{M_{D}(p)}$ as $p\to 0$ .

We will show that the components of this flat limit have multiplicity $1$ and are of the form $\mathcal{O}_{M_{1}},\ldots,\mathcal{O}_{M_{k}}$ for certain $d\times n$ matrices $M_{1},\ldots,M_{k}$ . We can take $M_{1}=M_{D}(0)$ if $\mathcal{O}_{M_{D}(0)}$ is nonzero. Theorem 6.2 below, which is the main result of this section, describes the sibling orbits $\mathcal{O}_{M_{1}},\ldots,\mathcal{O}_{M_{k}}$ . It states that the matrices $M_{i}$ arise from a particular “regular subdivision” of $P$ , and they are all what we call “orb-limits” of $M_{D}$ .

#### Definition 6.1.

Given a convex polytope $P$ , a subdivision of $P$ is a decomposition $P=P_{1}\cup\ldots\cup P_{k}$ into convex polytopes of the same dimension where each pairwise intersection $P_{i}\cap P_{j}$ is either empty or a common proper face of $P_{i}$ and $P_{j}$ . The faces of the $P_{i}$ are called the faces of the subdivision, and the polytopes $P_{i}$ are called the facets of the subdivision.

#### Definition 6.2.

Let $P$ be a (possibly unbounded) convex polytope, and let $h:P\to\mathbb{R}$ be a piecewise affine convex function. Denote by $P^{h}$ for the lower convex hull of $\{(p,h(p))\mid p\in P\}\subset P\times\mathbb{R}$ . The facets of $P^{h}$ each have dimension $\dim(P)$ , and the projections of these facets to $P$ form a subdivision of $P$ , called the regular subdivision of $P$ with lifting function $h$ .

If $P$ is bounded, then given a function $h:{\operatorname{Vert}}(P)\to\mathbb{R}$ , we define $P^{h}$ as the lower convex hull of $\{(v,h(v))\mid v\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(P)\}\subset P\times\mathbb{R}$ and as above use the facets of $P^{h}$ to define the regular subdivison of $P$ with lifting function $h$ . Extending $h$ to a piecewise affine convex function on all of $P$ by defining $h(p)\in\mathbb{R}$ as the unique value such that $(p,h(p))\in P^{h}$ induces the same $P^{h}$ and regular subdivision.

#### Remark 6.1.

Adding an affine function to $h$ or multiplying it by a positive scalar yields the same decomposition of $P$ .

#### Definition 6.3.

Define the height function $h_{M_{D}}:{\operatorname{Vert}}(P)\to\mathbb{Z}$ by

$$ h_{M_{D}}(v)=\operatorname{ord}_{t}\det(M_{D}^{v}) $$

where for a matrix $M$ and a subset of columns $v$ , we define $M^{v}$ to be the restriction of $M$ to the $v$ columns.

#### Definition 6.4.

We say that $M_{D}$ simply orb-limits to a matrix $M$ if there exist maps $\gamma_{T}:D\setminus\{0\}\to T$ and $\gamma_{GL}:D\setminus\{0\}\to GL_{d}$ such that $M=\lim_{p\to 0}\gamma_{GL}(p)M_{D}(p)\gamma_{T}(p)$ . We say that $M_{D}$ orb-limits to a matrix $M$ if $M_{D}$ simply orb-limits to $M$ after pulling back to a finite cover by a nonsingular curve (possibly everywhere ramified) of an open neighborhood of $0\in D$ .

We note that if $M_{D}$ orb-limits or simply orb-limits to a matrix $M$ , then it also does so after pulling back to a finite cover by a nonsingular curve (possibly everywhere ramified) of an open neighborhood of $0\in D$ .

Recall that $\mathcal{O}_{M}$ was defined in such a way that it is either zero or of dimension $(r+1)d-1$ .

#### Theorem 6.2.

Let $D$ be a smooth affine $1$ -dimensional $K$ -scheme of finite type, let $0\in D$ be a closed point, and let $t$ be a uniformizing parameter for $D$ around $0$ . Let $M_{D}:D\to\mathbb{A}^{d\times n}$ be a morphism that maps the generic point of $D$ to a rank $d$ matrix with no identically zero column.

Consider the map $\psi:\mathbb{P}^{(r+1)\times d-1}\times D\dashrightarrow(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n}\times D$ given by $(\widetilde{A},p)\mapsto(\widetilde{AM_{D}(p)},p)$ . Let $U\subset\mathbb{P}^{(r+1)\times d-1}\times(D\setminus\{0\})$ be a dense open subset of the domain of definition of $\psi$ , and let $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}$ be the family $\overline{\psi(U)}\subset(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n}\times D$ . Then

- (a) The family $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}$ is locally flat over $0\in D$ .

- (b) The fiber of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}$ over a general point $p\in D$ set-theoretically contains $\mathcal{O}_{M_{D}(p)}$ , and it is equal (as an algebraic cycle) to $\mathcal{O}_{M_{D}(p)}$ if it is $((r+1)d-1)$ -dimensional.

- (c) Suppose that $M_{D}$ orb-limits to matrices $M_{1},\ldots,M_{k}$ whose rank polytopes are the facets of the regular subdivision of $P$ induced by the lifting function $h_{M_{D}}$ . (The existence of the $M_{i}$ is guaranteed by Lemma 6.9.) Then the fiber of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}$ over $0\in D$ is equal to

$$ \bigcup_{i=1}^{k}\mathcal{O}_{M_{i}} $$

as an $((r+1)d-1)$ -dimensional algebraic cycle.

Because the fibers of a flat family of cycles in $(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n}$ have the same equivariant Chow class, Theorem 6.2 has the following immediate corollary.

#### Corollary 6.3.

Suppose that $M_{D}$ orb-limits to matrices $M_{1},\ldots,M_{k}$ whose rank polytopes are the facets of the regular subdivision of $P$ induced by the lifting function $h_{M_{D}}$ . (The existence of the $M_{i}$ is guaranteed by Lemma 6.9.) Let $p\in D$ be a general point. Then we have the equality of equivariant Chow classes

$$ \displaystyle[\mathcal{O}_{M_{D}(p)}]=\sum_{i=1}^{k}[\mathcal{O}_{M_{i}}]. $$

The remainder of this section is dedicated to the proof of Theorem 6.2.

### 6.1. Non-equivariant additivity

We now prove that the non-equivariant class $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ is additive (See Section 2.1), which is needed in the proof of Theorem 6.2. In the next section, we will use Theorem 6.2 to show that the equivariant class $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ is also additive.

#### Definition 6.5.

Let $d,n\geq 0$ be integers. Let $T(d,n)$ to be the abelian group generated by the indicator functions $1_{P_{M}}$ of rank polytopes of $d\times n$ matrices, modulo functions whose support has codimension at least $1$ in $\Delta$ . For a $d\times n$ matrix $M$ , we define $\langle M\rangle$ to be the class of $1_{P_{M}}$ in $T(d,n)$ .

Let $Z$ be an abelian group. Note that a map of sets $\phi:K^{d\times n}\to Z$ is additive if there is an abelian group homomorphism $\tilde{\phi}:T(d,n)\to Z$ such that $\tilde{\phi}(\langle M\rangle)=\phi(M)$ for all matrices $M\in K^{d\times n}$ . Observe that if such a map exists, it is unique.

#### Remark 6.4.

If $\phi$ is additive, then $\phi(M)$ depends only on the matroid of $M$ , and $\phi(M)=0$ if $P_{M}$ has positive codimension in $\Delta$ . This in particular occurs if ${\rm rk}(M)<d$ .

#### Remark 6.5.

If $P_{M}=P_{M_{1}}\cup\ldots\cup P_{M_{k}}$ is a subdivision, then $\langle M\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\langle M_{i}\rangle.$

#### Theorem 6.6.

For each $r$ , the association $M\mapsto[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ of $d\times n$ matrices to non-equivariant Chow classes is additive.

#### Proof.

Suppose $M_{1},\ldots,M_{k}$ are $d\times n$ matrices with $\sum_{i=1}^{k}a_{i}\langle M_{i}\rangle=0$ . By Theorem 5.2, the coefficient of $\prod_{i=1}^{n}H_{i}^{r-e_{i}}$ in $\sum_{i=1}^{k}a_{i}[\mathcal{O}_{M_{i}}]$ is given by

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{k}a_{i}1_{(r+1)P_{M_{i}}}(e_{1}+\epsilon_{1},\ldots,e_{n}+\epsilon_{n}) $$

for any $0<\epsilon_{1},\ldots,\epsilon_{n}$ with $\sum\epsilon_{i}=1$ . Since $\sum_{i=1}^{k}a_{i}\langle M_{i}\rangle=0$ , the sum $\sum_{i=1}^{k}a_{i}1_{(r+1)P_{M_{i}}}$ is supported on a subset of $(r+1)\Delta$ with codimension at least $1$ in $(r+1)\Delta$ . Hence we can find $\epsilon_{1},\ldots,\epsilon_{n}$ with $\sum_{i=1}^{k}a_{i}1_{(r+1)P_{M_{i}}}(e_{1}+\epsilon_{1},\ldots,e_{n}+\epsilon_{n})=0$ . Therefore $\sum_{i=1}^{k}a_{i}[\mathcal{O}_{M_{i}}]=0$ as no monomial can appear in its expansion. ∎

#### Corollary 6.7.

The equivariant Chow class $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ is zero if $P_{M}$ has positive codimension in $\Delta$ . Also, if $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]=0$ then $[\mathcal{O}_{M^{\prime}}]=0$ for all $M^{\prime}$ with the same matroid as $M$ .

#### Proof.

For the first part, by Theorem 6.6 we have the non-equivariant class $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]=0$ . Since $\mathcal{O}_{M}$ is effective, it follows that $\mathcal{O}_{M}=0$ , so the equivariant class $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]=0$ .

For the second part, if $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]=0$ , then $[\mathcal{O}_{M^{\prime}}]=0$ non-equivariantly, so $[\mathcal{O}_{M^{\prime}}]=0$ equivariantly by the same argument. ∎

#### Remark 6.8.

The matrix $M$ is connected if and only if $P_{M}$ is full-dimensional in $\Delta$ .

### 6.2. Regular subdivisions arising from degenerations

The following lemma connects degenerations of generalized matrix orbits and regular subdivisions of rank polytopes.

#### Lemma 6.9.

Let $F$ be a nonempty face of the regular subdivision of $P$ with lifting function $h_{M_{D}}$ . Then $M_{D}$ orb-limits to some matrix $M$ with $P_{M}=F$ .

#### Proof.

As in the definition of a regular subdivision, extend $h_{M_{D}}$ to a function on all of $P$ , and let $P^{h}\subset P\times\mathbb{R}$ be the lower convex hull of $\{(v,h_{M_{D}}(v))\mid v\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(P)\}$ . Because $F$ is the projection of a face of $P^{h}$ , there exists an affine function $L_{i,F}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}$ defined over $\mathbb{Q}$ such that $L_{F}(p)\leq h_{M_{D}}(p)$ for all $p\in P$ and $F=\{p\in P\mid L_{F}(p)=h_{M_{D}}(p)\}$ . There exists a positive integer $N$ such that $L_{F}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i,F}x_{i}+c_{F}$ for constants $c_{F},a_{i,F}\in\frac{1}{N}\mathbb{Z}$ .

Let $\widetilde{D}\to D$ be a finite cover with $\widetilde{D}$ nonsingular and a choice of point $\widetilde{0}$ mapping to $0$ such that the uniformizing parameter $s$ around $\widetilde{0}$ has $\operatorname{ord}_{s}(t)=N$ . Then the height function of the composition $M_{\widetilde{D}}:\tilde{D}\to D\to\mathbb{A}^{d\times n}$ is $Nh_{M_{D}}$ . Therefore, by pulling back to this cover, we may assume $c_{F},a_{i,F}\in\mathbb{Z}$ for all $1\leq i\leq n$ .

Define $\gamma_{T}:D\setminus\{0\}\to T\cong(K^{\times})^{n}$ by $(t^{-a_{1,F}},\ldots,t^{-a_{n,F}})$ . Let $\pi_{{\rm Gr}}:\mathbb{A}^{d\times n}\dashrightarrow{\operatorname{Gr}}(d,n)$ be the map sending a matrix $M$ to the span of the rows of $M$ . Consider the morphism $M_{D}\gamma_{T}:D\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb{A}^{d\times n}$ given by pointwise multiplication. The composite $\pi_{{\rm Gr}}\circ(M_{D}\gamma_{T}):D\setminus\{0\}\to{\operatorname{Gr}}(d,n)$ extends uniquely to $D$ because ${\operatorname{Gr}}(d,n)$ is projective.

The map $\pi$ restricted to rank $d$ matrices is a principal $GL_{d}$ -bundle with Zariski-local trivialization. Hence there exists an open neighborhood $U\subset{\operatorname{Gr}}(d,n)$ of $(\pi_{{\rm Gr}}\circ(M_{D}\gamma_{T}))(0)$ such that there exists a trivialization $\pi_{{\rm Gr}}^{-1}(U)\cong U\times GL_{d}$ . Let $\pi_{GL}:\pi_{{\rm Gr}}^{-1}(U)\to GL_{d}$ be the coordinate projection of this trivialization, which is $GL_{d}$ -equivariant. We may assume that the image of $M_{D}\gamma_{T}:D\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb{A}^{d\times n}$ lies in $\pi_{{\rm Gr}}^{-1}(U)$ by replacing $D$ with a suitable open subset. This yields a morphism

$$ \displaystyle\pi_{GL}\circ(M_{D}\gamma_{T}):D\setminus\{0\}\to GL_{d}. $$

Let $\gamma_{GL}$ be the composition of $\pi_{GL}\circ(M_{D}\gamma_{T})$ with the inverse map $GL_{d}\to GL_{d}$ .

Let $M^{\prime}_{D}:D\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb{A}^{d\times n}$ be the pointwise product $\gamma_{GL}M_{D}\gamma_{T}$ . Then the image of $M^{\prime}_{D}$ is contained in $\pi_{{\rm Gr}}^{-1}(U)$ . We will show that $M^{\prime}_{D}$ extends uniquely to a map $D\to\pi_{{\rm Gr}}^{-1}(U)$ , which we also call $M^{\prime}_{D}$ by abuse of notation.

To show this, it suffices to show that the compositions $\pi_{{\rm Gr}}\circ M^{\prime}_{D}:D\setminus\{0\}\to U$ and $\pi_{GL}\circ M^{\prime}_{D}:D\setminus\{0\}\to GL_{d}$ extend uniquely to $D$ . Observe that $\pi_{{\rm Gr}}\circ M^{\prime}_{D}=\pi_{{\rm Gr}}\circ(M_{D}\gamma_{T})$ , which we have already extended uniquely to $U$ . Also, the map $\pi_{GL}\circ M^{\prime}_{D}:D\setminus\{0\}\to GL_{d}$ is given by

$$ \displaystyle\pi_{GL}\circ(\gamma_{GL}M_{D}\gamma_{T})=\gamma_{GL}(\pi_{GL}\circ(M_{D}\gamma_{T}))=(\pi_{GL}\circ(M_{D}\gamma_{T}))^{-1}(\pi_{GL}\circ(M_{D}\gamma_{T}))=I, $$

the constant map sending each point of the curve $D\setminus\{0\}$ to the identity. This manifestly extends uniquely to $D$ , so there is an extension $M^{\prime}_{D}:D\to\pi_{{\rm Gr}}^{-1}(U)$ .

Define

$$ M=M^{\prime}_{D}(0)=\lim_{p\to 0}\gamma_{GL}(p)M_{D}(p)\gamma_{T}(p), $$

which is an orb-limit of $M_{D}$ . Then $M\in\pi_{{\rm Gr}}^{-1}(U)$ , so it has full rank. For any vertex $v$ of $P$ we have

$$ \det((M^{\prime}_{D})^{v})=\det\gamma_{GL}\cdot\det M_{D}\cdot t^{-\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i,F}v_{i}} $$

so

$$ \operatorname{ord}_{t}\det((M^{\prime}_{D})^{v})=\operatorname{ord}_{t}(\det\gamma_{GL})+h_{M_{D}}(v)-\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i,F}v_{i}. $$

Observe that since $M^{\prime}_{D}(0)$ exists and has full rank, the minimum value of $\operatorname{ord}_{t}\det((M^{\prime}_{D})^{v})$ over all vertices $v\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(P)$ is $0$ . Hence $\operatorname{ord}_{t}(\det\gamma_{GL})=-c_{F}$ . Now $\det(M^{v})\neq 0$ if and only if $\operatorname{ord}_{t}\det((M^{\prime}_{D})^{v})=0$ , and this happens exactly when $h_{M_{D}}(v)=L_{F}(v)$ , i.e. $v\in F$ . Hence, the rank polytope of $M$ is $F$ , as desired. ∎

Hence, we have some information about the special fibers of degenerations of generalized matrix orbits. Now we want to understand the general fibers. The following technical lemma is necessary to compare images of general fibers of a family with general fibers of the image of a family.

#### Lemma 6.10.

Let $S$ be a Noetherian integral $K$ -scheme. Suppose that $X,Y$ are finite type schemes over $S$ such that $X\to S$ has integral general fiber. Let $\phi:X\to Y$ be a morphism of $S$ -schemes that is generically finite onto its image. Then for $s\in S$ general, the scheme-theoretic image of $\phi|_{s}$ agrees with the fiber of the scheme-theoretic image of $\phi$ over $s$ .

#### Proof.

Without loss of generality, we can restrict $S$ so the fibers of $X\to S$ are equidimensional [50, Tag 05F7]. The scheme-theoretic image of $\phi$ is $\overline{\phi(X)}$ with the induced reduced subscheme structure [50, Tag 056B]. It is clear that the scheme-theoretic image of $\phi|_{s}$ is contained in the fiber of $\overline{\phi(X)}$ over $s$ . To show the other inclusion, we claim the geometric generic fiber of $\overline{\phi(X)}$ over $S$ is integral [17, IV 12.1.1 (x)].

Let ${\rm Spec}(\overline{L})\to S$ be the geometric generic point. Scheme-theoretic image of a quasicompact morphism commutes with flat base change [50, Tag 081I], so the scheme-theoretic image of $\phi$ pulled back to $Y\times_{S}{\rm Spec}(\overline{L})$ agrees with the scheme-theoretic image of the induced map $X\times_{S}{\rm Spec}(\overline{L})\to Y\times_{S}{\rm Spec}(\overline{L})$ , which is integral.

Therefore, the general fiber of $\overline{\phi(X)}$ over $S$ is integral [50, Tag 0551]. Therefore, we can restrict $S$ so that every fiber of $\overline{\phi(X)}$ over $S$ is integral. Then, by dimension reasons, this shows that the scheme-theoretic image of $\phi|_{s}$ is equal to the fiber of $\overline{\phi(X)}$ over $s$ . ∎

We are now ready to prove Theorem 6.2.

#### Proof of Theorem 6.2.

Part (a) follows directly from $\psi(U)\subset(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n}\times(D\setminus\{0\})$ .

Next, we prove (b). Given a general $\widetilde{A}\in\mathbb{P}^{(r+1)\times d-1}$ , we have $(\widetilde{AM_{D}(p)},p)\in\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}$ . It follows that the fiber of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}$ over $p\in D$ set-theoretically contains $\mathcal{O}_{M_{D}(p)}$ . If the fiber of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}$ over $p$ is $((r+1)d-1)$ -dimensional, then the map $\psi$ is generically finite onto its image. We claim that $\psi$ is generically injective. Indeed, assume that $\psi(\widetilde{A},p^{\prime})=\psi(\widetilde{B},p^{\prime})$ is a general element of ${\rm im}(\psi)$ for $(r+1)\times d$ matrices $A,B$ and $p^{\prime}\in D$ . Then this is further equal to $\psi(\widetilde{A+\lambda B},p^{\prime})$ for general $\lambda$ , contradicting generic finiteness if $\widetilde{A}\neq\widetilde{B}$ . Hence, by Lemma 6.10, the fiber of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}$ over $p$ is the closure of the image of $\psi|_{(\mathbb{P}^{(r+1)\times d-1}\times\{p\})\cap U}$ , which is $\mathcal{O}_{M_{D}(p)}$ .

Finally, we prove (c). We claim that the fiber $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_{0}$ contains each $\mathcal{O}_{M_{i}}$ . By replacing $D$ with a suitable finite cover by a nonsingular curve and $M_{D}$ with an extension to $D$ of $\gamma_{GL}M_{D}\gamma_{T}$ for suitable $\gamma_{GL}:D\setminus\{0\}\to GL_{r+1}$ and $\gamma_{T}:D\setminus\{0\}\to T$ , we may assume that $M=M_{D}(0)$ . Given a general $\tilde{A}\in\mathbb{P}^{(r+1)\times d-1}$ , we have $(\widetilde{AM_{D}(p)},p)\in\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}$ for general $p\in D$ . Taking the limit as $p\to 0$ yields $(\widetilde{AM_{D}(0)},0)\in\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}$ . Since $\tilde{A}$ is general, it follows that the fiber of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}$ over $0\in D$ set-theoretically contains $\mathcal{O}_{M_{i}}$ as desired.

Now, we claim that the nonzero $\mathcal{O}_{M_{i}}$ are distinct. Assume to the contrary that $\mathcal{O}_{M_{i}}=\mathcal{O}_{M_{j}}\neq 0$ for some $1\leq i<j\leq k$ . Then the non-equivariant classes satisfy $[\mathcal{O}_{M_{i}}]=[\mathcal{O}_{M_{j}}]\neq 0$ . By Theorem 5.2, there exists $(e_{1},\ldots,e_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ such that for any $0<\epsilon_{1},\ldots,\epsilon_{n}$ with $\sum_{i=1}^{n}\epsilon_{i}=1$ we have $(e_{1}+\epsilon_{1},\ldots,e_{n}+\epsilon_{n})$ is contained in $(r+1)(P_{M_{i}}\cap P_{M_{j}})$ . But $(r+1)(P_{M_{i}}\cap P_{M_{j}})$ has codimension at least $1$ in the hyperplane $\{\sum x_{i}=(r+1)d\}$ , so we cannot have the containment for all choices of $\epsilon_{i}$ .

Since $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_{0}$ contains each $\mathcal{O}_{M_{i}}$ , the $((r+1)d-1)$ -dimensional algebraic cycle

$$ Z=\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_{0}-\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{O}_{M_{i}} $$

is effective. The nonzero $\mathcal{O}_{M_{i}}$ are distinct and irreducible of dimension $(r+1)d-1$ and $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}$ is locally flat at $0\in D$ , so we have the equality of non-equivariant Chow classes

$$ [Z]=[\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_{0}]-\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\mathcal{O}_{M_{i}}]=[\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_{p}]-\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\mathcal{O}_{M_{i}}]=[\mathcal{O}_{M_{D}(p)}]-\sum_{i=1}^{n}[\mathcal{O}_{M_{i}}]=0 $$

for $p$ general, where the third equality follows from (b) and the fourth equality follows from Theorem 6.6. Hence $Z=0$ , as desired. ∎

## 7. Additivity of $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$

In this section, we prove part of Theorem 2, by showing that the association $M\mapsto[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ is additive (see Section 2.1 and Definition 6.5) using the algorithm implicit in [16, Appendix A] and results from Section 6 and Appendix A. This will be used to reduce the computation of $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ to simpler generalized matrix orbit classes in later sections.

#### Theorem 7.1.

For each $r$ , the association $M\mapsto[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ of $d\times n$ matrices to equivariant Chow classes is additive.

Additivity of equivariant Chow classes of torus orbits in the Grassmannian is known using [37, Proposition 1.9] to specialize the result in equivariant K-theory [23, Example 3.5] to equivariant Chow classes [9, Section 2.2]. However, this is insufficient for our purposes.

Even the fact that $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ depends only on the matroid of $M$ is far from obvious. The realization spaces of matroids should be expected to be poorly behaved in general by Mnev universality [36, Theorem 1.3] [44], and there are explicit examples of disconnected realization spaces of line arrangements [1, 6, 27, 45].

### 7.1. Outline of the proof of Theorem 7.1

Let $S(d,n)$ be the abelian group generated by indicator functions of all (possibly unbounded) convex polytopal regions in $\{\sum x_{i}=d\}$ modulo functions whose support has positive codimension. We will be working exclusively inside $S(d,n)$ from now on, treating in particular $\langle M\rangle\in S(d,n)$ (recall Definition 6.5). For any (possibly unbounded) convex polytopal region $P$ , we will also write $\langle P\rangle$ for the class of $1_{P}$ inside $S(d,n)$ .

In [16, Appendix A], Derksen and Fink show using an explicit algorithm that if $\sum_{i=1}^{k}a_{i}\langle M_{i}\rangle=0$ then the expression $\sum_{i=1}^{k}a_{i}\langle P_{M_{i}}\rangle$ can be reduced to $0$ by using replacements $\langle P^{\prime}\rangle\mapsto 0$ when $P^{\prime}$ is of positive codimension inside $\{\sum x_{i}=d\}$ , and replacements $\langle P\rangle\mapsto\langle P+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v\rangle-\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\langle P_{i}\rangle$ with $v=e_{i}-e_{j}$ with $i>j$ , where $P+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v=P\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^{\ell}P_{i}$ are certain subdivisions which we will call “shadow facet subdivisions” (see Lemma 7.4). We will show that each polytope appearing in the algorithm is of the form $P_{M}+C$ where $(M,C)$ is an “admissible pair”, which we define below.

As in Appendix A, we define a matroidal cone to be a cone $C$ generated by rays of the form $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}(e_{i}-e_{j})$ .

#### Definition 7.1.

Let $M$ be a $d\times n$ matrix and let $C$ be a matroidal cone. We define the associated polytope of $(M,C)$ to be the polytope $P_{M}+C\subset\{\sum x_{i}=d\}$ . We say that $(M,C)$ is an admissible pair if $P_{M}+C$ is full-dimensional in $\{\sum x_{i}=d\}$ and $(P_{M}+C)\cap\Delta=P_{M}$ .

The criterion for $(M,C)$ to be admissible implies that if $e_{i}-e_{j}\in C$ , then the $i$ th column of $M$ is morally speaking more general than the $j$ th column of $M$ .

We will augment Derksen and Fink’s algorithm, replacing each polytope $P$ with an admissible pair $(M,C)$ with associated polytope $P$ . This replacement will be done in such a way that if $P+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v=P\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^{\ell}P_{i}$ is a subdivision used in the algorithm, then $[\mathcal{O}_{M^{\prime}}]=[\mathcal{O}_{M}]+\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}[\mathcal{O}_{M_{i}}]$ , where $(M^{\prime},C^{\prime})$ is the admissible pair associated to $P+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v$ and $(M_{i},C_{i})$ is the admissible pair associated to $P_{i}$ . We will accomplish this using explicit degenerations over $\mathbb{A}^{1}_{t}$ (see Theorem 6.2) which are linear in $t$ and add $t$ times general multiples of certain columns of $M$ to other columns.

As it turns out, applying the rewriting procedure of Derksen and Fink without combining or cancelling any codimension zero terms allows us to rewrite any $\langle M\rangle$ as a linear combination $\sum\epsilon_{i}\langle P_{i}\rangle$ , where each $P_{i}$ is a “strictly positive matroidal cone” with apex in $\Delta$ and $\epsilon_{i}=\pm 1$ .

#### Definition 7.2.

We define a positive matroidal cone $C$ to be a matroidal cone $C$ whose generating vectors $e_{i}-e_{j}$ have $i>j$ . We define a strictly positive matroidal cone $C$ to be an $(n-1)$ -dimensional positive matroidal cone generated by $n-1$ vectors $e_{j}-e_{\alpha_{j}}$ with $\alpha_{j}<j$ and $j\in\{2,\ldots,n\}$ .

The key fact about translates of strictly positive matroidal cones is that there are no relations between them in $S(d,n)$ , so if we rewrite the expression $\sum a_{i}\langle M_{i}\rangle$ as $\sum\epsilon_{i}\langle P_{i}\rangle$ where each $P_{i}$ is a strictly positive matroidal cone with apex in $\Delta$ , then the sum of the coefficients in front of a given $\langle P\rangle$ is zero. We then deduce the theorem from the fact for any matroidal cone $P$ with apex in $\Delta$ , the space of all matrices $M$ such that $P_{M}=P\cap\Delta$ is connected, so $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]=[\mathcal{O}_{M^{\prime}}]$ whenever $P_{M}=P_{M^{\prime}}=P\cap\Delta$ .

### 7.2. Invariance of $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ when $P_{M}=(v+C)\cap\Delta$

In this subsection, we prove that if $v\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(\Delta)$ and $C$ is a matroidal cone, then all matrices $M$ with $P_{M}=(v+C)\cap\Delta$ have the same $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ . We also prove Proposition 7.3, which serves as one of the key combinatorial interpretations of all future degenerations.

#### Definition 7.3.

We define a polytope $P\subset\Delta$ to be a cone-like matroid polytope if there is a matroidal cone $C$ and vertex $v\in\Delta$ for which $P=(v+C)\cap\Delta$ .

#### Lemma 7.2.

Let $M,M^{\prime}$ be $d\times n$ matrices. Assume $\mathcal{O}_{M}\neq 0$ . Suppose that $P_{M}=P_{M^{\prime}}=(v+C)\cap\Delta$ is a cone-like matroid polytope. Then

- (a) There exists an open subset $U\subset\mathbb{A}^{1}_{t}$ containing $0$ and $1$ , a path $M_{U}:U\to\mathbb{A}^{d\times n}$ satisfying $M_{U}(0)=M$ and $M_{U}(1)=M^{\prime}$ , and a flat degeneration $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\subset(\mathbb{P}^{d-1})^{n}\times U$ such that $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_{p}=\mathcal{O}_{M_{D}(p)}$ as $((r+1)d-1)$ -dimensional cycles for all $p\in U$ .

- (b) $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]=[\mathcal{O}_{M^{\prime}}]$ .

In order to prove Lemma 7.2, we will need to understand the structure of cone-like matroid polytopes. We will do this in a much greater generality than will be needed at this moment.

#### Proposition 7.3.

Let $M$ be a $d\times n$ rank $d$ matrix and let $C$ be a matroidal cone. Define the $n\times n$ matrix $B$ by

$$ B_{i,k}=\begin{cases}\lambda_{i,k}&\mbox{if $e_{k}-e_{i}\in C$ and $k\neq i$}\\
0&\mbox{otherwise}\end{cases} $$

where the $\lambda_{i,k}$ are general elements of $K$ . Let $N=M(1+tB)$ .

- (a) For any $z\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(\Delta)$ , the order ${\operatorname{ord}}_{t}\det(N^{z})$ is the minimum value of $|z\setminus w|$ over all pairs $(w,\phi)$ such that $w\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(P_{M})$ and $\phi:z\setminus w\to w\setminus z$ is a bijection with $e_{k}-e_{\phi(k)}\in C$ for all $k\in z\setminus w$ . In particular, it is $\infty$ if and only if no such pair exists.

- (b) For general $t$ , the rank polytope of $N$ is $(P_{A}+C)\cap\Delta$ .

#### Proof.

We first prove (a). For any $w,z\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(\Delta)$ , let $(1+tB)^{z}_{w}$ denote the submatrix of $1+tB$ formed by the columns in $z$ and the rows in $w$ . By the Cauchy-Binet formula, $\det(N^{z})=\det(M(1+tB)^{z})$ is given by

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{w\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(\Delta)}\det(M^{w})\det((1+tB)^{z}_{w}) \displaystyle=\sum_{w\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(P_{A})}\det(M^{w})\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\phi:z\to w\\
\text{bijection}\end{subarray}}\pm\prod_{k\in z}(1+tB)_{\phi(k),k} \displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}w\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(P_{M})\\
\phi:z\to w\\
\text{bijection}\end{subarray}}\pm\det(M^{w})\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\in z\\
\phi(k)\neq k\end{subarray}}(tB_{\phi(k),k}). $$

Because each $\lambda_{i,k}$ is general, all nonzero terms of this sum are linearly independent. Hence ${\operatorname{ord}}_{t}\det(N^{z})$ is the minimum value of $|\{k\in z\mid\phi(k)\neq k\}|$ over all pairs $(w,\phi)$ , where $w\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(P_{A})$ and $\phi:z\to w$ is a bijection such that $e_{k}-e_{\phi(k)}\in C$ for all $k\in z$ . In particular, it is $\infty$ if and only if no such pair exists.

If ${\operatorname{ord}}_{t}\det(N^{z})=\infty$ , then (a) clearly holds. Otherwise, we claim that there exists a pair $(w,\phi)$ attaining the minimum value of $|\{k\in z\mid\phi(k)\neq k\}|$ such that $\phi$ fixes $z\cap w$ . Indeed, suppose $(w,\phi^{\prime})$ minimizes $|\{k\in z\mid\phi(k)\neq k\}|$ . Define $\phi$ by

$$ \phi(i)=\begin{cases}i&\text{if $i\in z\cap w$, and}\\
(\phi^{\prime})^{k_{i}}(i)&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} $$

where $k_{i}$ is the smallest number such that $(\phi^{\prime})^{k_{i}}(i)\in w\setminus z$ . It is clear that $\phi$ is a bijection fixing $z\cap w$ , and $e_{i}-e_{\phi(i)}\in C$ as $C$ is closed under addition. This shows part (a), and part (b) now follows from Lemma A.3. ∎

#### Proof of Lemma 7.2.

As $\mathcal{O}_{M}\neq 0$ , by Corollary 6.7, all generalized matrix orbits with matroid $(v+C)\cap\Delta$ are nonzero.

First, we prove (a). Let $C^{\prime}$ be the nonnegative span of $\{e_{j}-e_{i}\in C\mid j\not\in v,i\in v\}$ . By Lemma A.3, we have $(v+C)\cap\Delta=(v+C^{\prime})\cap\Delta$ . Hence, by replacing $C$ with $C^{\prime}$ , we may assume that if $e_{j}-e_{i}\in C$ for $i\neq j$ , then $j\not\in v$ and $i\in v$ . We can multiply $M$ and $M^{\prime}$ on the left by elements of $GL_{d}$ and assume that $M^{v}=(M^{\prime})^{v}=I$ . We can also assume $v=e_{1}+\cdots+e_{d}$ .

Now, we consider the locus $Z_{M}\subset\mathbb{A}^{d\times n}$ of $d\times n$ matrices whose underlying matroid has polytope $P_{M}$ and whose restriction to the leftmost $d\times d$ submatrix is the identity. We claim that, for all $N\in Z_{M}$ , if $e_{j}-e_{i}\not\in C$ then $N_{ij}=0$ . Indeed, if $N_{ij}\neq 0$ , then as $M^{v}=I$ , replacing $i$ in the set $\{1,\ldots,d\}$ with $j$ preserves linear independence, so

$$ \displaystyle v+(e_{j}-e_{i})=(e_{1}+\cdots+e_{d})+(e_{j}-e_{i})\in P_{M}\subset v+C, $$

and hence $e_{j}-e_{i}\in C$ . Therefore, the affine subspace $L_{M}\subset\mathbb{A}^{d\times n}$ consisting of matrices $N$ where $N_{ii}=1$ and $N_{ij}=0$ if $e_{j}-e_{i}\notin C$ contains $Z_{M}$ .

We have that $Z_{M}$ is a locally closed set in $L_{M}$ because it can be defined by the vanishing and non-vanishing of minors. The inclusion $Z_{M}\subset L_{M}$ is dense by Proposition 7.3(b) applied to the $d\times n$ matrix $A$ with $A_{ii}=1$ and $A_{ij}=0$ if $i\neq j$ , so $Z_{M}$ is open.

In Theorem 6.2, choose $D=\mathbb{A}^{1}_{t}$ and $M_{D}(t)=tM+(1-t)M^{\prime}$ . By choosing $U\subset\mathbb{P}^{(r+1)\times d-1}\times(M_{D}^{-1}(Z_{M})\setminus\{0,1\})$ , we obtain a family $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}$ that is flat over both $0\in D$ and $1\in D$ . Part (a) of the lemma follows, and part (b) follows immediately from part (a). ∎

### 7.3. Regular subdivisions arising from unbounded polytope decompositions

In this subsection, we will describe particular regular subdivisions $P=\bigcup_{i=1}^{k}P_{i}$ of possibly unbounded polytopes. Each such regular subdivision yields a decomposition $P\cap\Delta=\bigcup_{i=1}^{k}(P_{i}\cap\Delta)$ of bounded polytopes, which becomes a regular subdivision after removing lower-dimensional terms from the right-hand side. We will then use these regular subdivisions to construct the remaining degenerations $M_{D}$ that will be used in the proof of Theorem 7.1.

#### Lemma 7.4.

Given a convex (possibly unbounded) full-dimensional polytope $P$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and a nonzero vector $v$ , we have a regular subdivision of $P+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v$ induced by the piecewise affine function $h:z\mapsto\inf_{\lambda}\{\lambda|z-\lambda v\in P\}$ . The subdivision consists of $P$ and all polytopes $F+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v$ , where $F$ ranges over facets of $P$ such that $(F+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v)\cap P=F$ .

#### Definition 7.4.

We call the facets of $P$ appearing in Lemma 7.4 shadow facets as in [16, Appendix A]. They are the upper facets with respect to the $v$ -direction. We further call the subdivision the shadow facet subdivision.

#### Proof of Lemma 7.4.

Define the linear map $\phi:\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}$ by $\phi(x,\lambda)=(x+\lambda v,\lambda)$ and define $Q=\phi(P\times\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0})$ . Note that $(y,\lambda)\in Q$ if and only if $\lambda\geq 0$ and $y-\lambda v\in P$ . Then, for any $x\in P+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v$ , the minimum of $\{\lambda\mid(x,\lambda)\in Q\}$ is exactly $h(x)$ . Hence, the lower convex hull of $Q$ is $P^{h}$ , so the facets of the regular subdivision of $P+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v$ induced by $h$ are the projections of the lower facets of $Q$ to $P+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v$ .

Because $\phi$ is a linear embedding, the facets of $Q$ are $\phi(P\times\{0\})$ and $\phi(F\times\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0})$ for the facets $F$ of $P$ . The facet $\phi(P\times\{0\})$ is a lower facet and $\phi(F\times\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0})$ is a lower facet if and only if $F$ is a shadow facet. Projecting these facets to $P+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v$ yields the shadow facet subdivision. ∎

We will now use Proposition 7.3 to construct the remaining degenerations needed in the proof of Theorem 7.1.

#### Theorem 7.5.

Let $(M,C)$ be an admissible pair and let $v=e_{i}-e_{j}$ with $i\neq j$ . Then there exists a regular map $M_{D}:\mathbb{A}^{1}_{t}\to\mathbb{A}^{d\times n}$ with $M_{D}(0)=M$ such that for general $s\in\mathbb{A}^{1}_{t}$ , there exist admissible pairs $(M_{1},C_{1}),\ldots,(M_{k},C_{k})$ , where each $M_{i}$ is an orb-limit of $M_{D}$ and

- (a) The pair $(M_{D}(s),C+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v)$ is admissible and $P_{M_{D}(s)}+(C+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v)=(P_{M}+C)+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v$ .

- (b) We have a decomposition

$$ P_{M_{D}(s)}+(C+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v)=(P_{M}+C)\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^{k}(P_{M_{i}}+C_{i}) $$

which is the shadow facet subdivision of $(P_{M}+C)+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v$ .

- (c) We have a decomposition

$$ P_{M_{D}(s)}=P_{M}\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^{k}P_{M_{i}} $$

which becomes the regular subdivision of $P_{M_{D}(s)}$ with lifting function $h_{M_{D}}$ associated to the degeneration $M_{D}$ after removing all terms of positive codimension in $P_{M_{D}(s)}$ .

- (d) We have

$$ [\mathcal{O}_{M_{D}(s)}]=[\mathcal{O}_{M}]+\sum_{i=1}^{k}[\mathcal{O}_{M_{i}}]. $$

#### Proof.

Define the $n\times n$ matrix $B$ by

$$ B_{i,k}=\begin{cases}\lambda_{i,k}&\mbox{if $e_{k}-e_{i}\in C+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v$ and $k\neq i$}\\
0&\mbox{otherwise}\end{cases} $$

where the $\lambda_{i,k}$ are general elements of $K$ . Define $M_{D}$ by $M_{D}(t)=M(1+tB)$ .

By Proposition 7.3, we have $P_{M_{D}(s)}=(P_{M}+(C+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v))\cap\Delta$ . Thus $P_{M_{D}(s)}+(C+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v)=(P_{M}+C)+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v$ , which proves (a).

Furthermore by Proposition 7.3 and Lemma A.4 we have that $h_{M_{D}}$ , when restricted to $\Delta$ , coincides with the height function of the shadow facet subdivision of $(P_{M}+C)+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v$ as given in Lemma 7.4. Hence, letting $F_{1},\ldots,F_{k}$ be the shadow facets of $P_{M}+C$ , we have that $(F_{i}+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v)\cap\Delta$ are faces of the regular subdivision of $P_{M_{D}(t)}$ with lifting function $h_{M_{D}}$ , and all facets of the regular subdivision apart from $P_{M}$ arise in this way. Each shadow facet $F_{i}$ is the Minkowski sum of a face of $P_{M}$ with a face of $C$ , so $F_{i}\cap\Delta\neq\emptyset$ . Therefore the faces $(F_{i}+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v)\cap\Delta$ are nonempty. By Lemma 6.9, for each $i$ , the degeneration $M_{D}$ orb-limits to a matrix $M_{i}$ such that $P_{M_{i}}=(F_{i}+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v)\cap\Delta$ . By definition of the $M_{i}$ , part (c) follows. Define $C_{i}=C_{F_{i}}+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v$ , where $C_{F_{i}}$ is the cone generated by the unbounded edges of $F_{i}$ .

We will now show that $P_{M_{i}}+C_{i}=F_{i}+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v$ , which by definition of $M_{i}$ implies that $(M_{i},C_{i})$ is admissible. Clearly $P_{M_{i}}+C_{i}\subset F_{i}+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v$ , so it remains to show that $F_{i}+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v\subset P_{M_{i}}+C_{i}$ . As $F_{i}$ is the Minkowski sum of a face of $P_{M}$ with a face of $C$ , we have $F_{i}=(F_{i}\cap P_{M})+C_{F_{i}}\subset P_{M_{i}}+C_{F_{i}}$ from which we conclude $F_{i}+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v\subset P_{M_{i}}+C_{i}$ . Along with (a), this in particular implies (b).

Finally, (d) follows from (c) and Corollary 6.3.

∎

### 7.4. The proof of Theorem 7.1

In this subsection, we prove Theorem 7.1. The final piece of data we need is the algorithm implicit in [16, Appendix A], which will be woven into the fabric of the proof.

#### Proof.

We proceed exactly as in Section 7.1. Corollary 6.7 allows us to safely discard any region of positive codimension in $\{\sum x_{i}=d\}$ , and starting with replacing $P_{M}$ with $(M,0)$ , Theorem 7.5 allows us to augment each step of the algorithm as described. Finally, Lemma 7.2 allows us to combine terms at the end when we reduce to strictly positive matroidal cones.

For the interested reader, we supply a sketch of the algorithm to reduce to translates of strictly positive matroidal cones and a proof that there are no relations in $S(d,n)$ between translates of strictly positive matroidal cones.

Define a positive matroidal polytope to be a polytope all of whose edges are in directions $e_{i}-e_{j}$ and all of whose unbounded edges are in directions $e_{i}-e_{j}$ with $i>j$ . For example, any rank polytope is a positive matroidal polytope. The algorithm proceeds in such a way that all polytopes described below are positive matroidal polytopes. Take constants $1\ll\lambda_{n}\ll\lambda_{n-1}\ll\cdots\ll\lambda_{1}$ . Given a polytope $P$ which appears in the algorithm, take $k\geq-1$ minimal such that $P^{k}=P\cap\bigcap_{i=n-k}^{n}\{x_{i}=\lambda_{i}\}$ is not a positive matroidal cone. If no such $k$ exists, then the direction vectors connecting the apexes of the cones $P^{\ell}$ for $\ell=-1,0,1,\ldots,n-1$ realize $P$ as a strictly positive matroidal cone. Otherwise, we claim that $P^{k}$ is a positive matroidal polytope. Indeed let $A$ be the set of indices $i$ for which $e_{n-k}-e_{i}$ is a direction vector contained inside the positive matroidal cone $P^{k-1}$ and let $C$ be the positive matroidal subcone of $P^{k-1}$ generated by those $e_{i}-e_{j}\in P^{k-1}$ with $i,j<n-k$ . Then for $v$ the apex of $P^{k-1}$ , we have $P^{k}=v+(\lambda_{n-k}-v_{n-k}){\operatorname{conv}}_{i\in A}(e_{n-k}-e_{i})+C$ . Hence since the edge directions of a Minkowski sum of polytopes are a subset of the edge directions of those polytopes (see Appendix A), the claim follows.

Since $P^{k}$ is a positive matroidal polytope that is not a positive matroidal cone, it is not a cone. Choose a bounded edge of $P^{k}$ , which by the above discussion is parallel to $e_{i}-e_{j}$ for some $i>j$ . In the shadow facet subdivision of $P^{k}+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v$ with $v=e_{i}-e_{j}$ , both the polytope $P^{k}+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v$ and the $P^{k}_{i}+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v$ for shadow facets $P^{k}_{i}$ have strictly fewer vertices than $P^{k}$ , as their vertices are all subsets of ${\operatorname{Vert}}(P)$ containing at most one of the two vertices of the chosen edge. Furthermore, this shadow facet decomposition is induced by the shadow facet decomposition of $P+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v$ after intersecting with $\bigcap_{i=n-k}^{n}\{x_{i}=\lambda_{i}\}$ , and the polytopes $P+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v$ and the $P_{i}$ remain cones up until this intersection. Hence as the number of vertices of the polytopes intersected with $\bigcap_{i=n-k}^{n}\{x_{i}=\lambda_{i}\}$ strictly decreases in each application, we will eventually reduce down to polytopes whose intersections with $\bigcap_{i=n-k}^{n}\{x_{i}=\lambda_{i}\}$ are positive matroidal cones. Since we can now decrement $k$ , we eventually reduce all polytopes to strictly positive matroidal cones.

Now, we argue why there are no relations between translates of strictly positive matroidal cones. Indeed, suppose we have a combination $\sum a_{i}\langle P_{i}\rangle=0$ . Then as the cones are positive matroidal, if one of these cones intersects a sufficiently small neighborhood of the lexicographically first vertex $v$ , then it has this vertex as an apex. By considering this small neighborhood of $v$ , we deduce that if we rectrict our sum to just those cones with apex $v$ we still get zero. By induction on the number of cones, we may assume that all cones have apex $v$ . Take $\lambda\gg 0$ , and consider the intersections with $x_{n}=\lambda$ . These intersections remain strictly positive matroidal cones, and $\sum a_{i}\langle P_{i}\cap\{x_{n}=\lambda\}\rangle=0$ in $S(d-\lambda,n-1)\times\{\lambda\}$ . Hence, we are done by induction on dimension. ∎

## 8. Parallel and Series Connection, Existence of Rational Functions

In this section, we show that the generalized matrix orbit classes of the series and parallel connection of two matrices (Definition 2.3) can be computed from the generalized matrix orbit classes of the matrices themselves (Theorem 8.1). Combining this with the additivity result of the previous section, we will prove that the generalized matrix orbit class of a matrix takes a very particular form (Theorem 8.2). In Section 9, we will combine Theorem 8.2 with the non-equivariant results of Section 5 to compute $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ for any matrix $M$ .

The next theorem, Theorem 3 from the introduction, relates the classes

$$ \displaystyle[\mathcal{O}_{M_{1}}] \displaystyle\in A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}((\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n_{1}})=A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}((\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n_{1}-1})\otimes A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r}) \displaystyle[\mathcal{O}_{M_{2}}] \displaystyle\in A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}((\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n_{2}})=A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})\otimes A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}((\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n_{2}-1}) \displaystyle[\mathcal{O}_{P(M_{1},M_{2})}] \displaystyle\in A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}((\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n_{1}+n_{2}-1})=A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}((\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n_{1}-1})\otimes A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})\otimes A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}((\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n_{2}-1}) \displaystyle[\mathcal{O}_{S(M_{1},M_{2})}] \displaystyle\in A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}((\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n_{1}+n_{2}-1})=A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}((\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n_{1}-1})\otimes A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})\otimes A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}((\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n_{2}-1}) $$

using the quantum product $\star$ from Section 2.3.

#### Theorem 8.1.

For $i\in\{1,2\}$ let $M_{i}$ be a $d_{i}\times n_{i}$ matrix. We have the equality of equivariant Chow classes

$$ [\mathcal{O}_{M_{1}}]\star[\mathcal{O}_{M_{2}}]=[\mathcal{O}_{P(M_{1},M_{2})}]+\hbar[\mathcal{O}_{S(M_{1},M_{2})}] $$

where the quantum product $\star$ is taken along the last factor of $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}((\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n_{1}})=A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}((\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n_{1}-1})\otimes A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})$ and the first factor of $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}((\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n_{2}})=A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}(\mathbb{P}^{r})\otimes A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}((\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n_{2}-1})$ .

#### Theorem 8.2.

For every matrix $M$ , there is a rational function $Q_{M}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},y_{1},\ldots,y_{n})$ independent of $r$ such that $Q_{M}(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n},F(z_{1}),\ldots,F(z_{n}))$ is a polynomial of degree at most $r$ in the indeterminates $z_{i}$ that yields $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ after substituting $z_{i}=H_{i}$ .

### 8.1. Parallel Connection and Series Connection

The goal of this subsection is to prove Theorem 8.1. We start by proving the parallel connection formula.

#### Lemma 8.3.

Let $p_{1}:(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n_{1}+n_{2}-1}\to(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n_{1}}$ be the projection to the first $n_{1}$ factors and let $p_{2}:(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n_{1}+n_{2}-1}\to(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n_{2}}$ be the projection to the last $n_{2}$ factors. Then we have

$$ p_{1}^{*}[\mathcal{O}_{M_{1}}]\cap p_{2}^{*}[\mathcal{O}_{M_{2}}]=[\mathcal{O}_{P(M_{1},M_{2})}]. $$

(Here we write the intersection product as $\cap$ to distinguish it from the quantum product $\star$ .)

Let $W_{1}=K^{n_{1}}$ and $W_{2}=K^{n_{2}}$ . Let $x_{1,1},\ldots,x_{1,n_{1}}\in W_{1}$ be the columns of $M_{1}$ and let $x_{2,1},\ldots,x_{2,n_{2}}\in W_{2}$ be the columns of $M_{2}$ . Define $W=(W_{1}\oplus W_{2})/\langle x_{1,n_{1}}-x_{2,1}\rangle=K^{n_{1}+n_{2}-1}$ . The columns of $P(M_{1},M_{2})$ are the vectors $x_{1,1},\ldots,x_{1,n_{1}}=x_{2,1},\ldots,x_{2,n_{2}}$ considered as elements of $W$ .

Let $V=K^{r+1}$ .
