## 12. Application: line sections of a hypersurface

We consider the following problem.

#### Problem 12.1.

For a general hypersurface $X\subset\mathbb{P}^{r}$ of degree $d$ with $d=2r+1$ , what is the degree of the map

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{X}:\mathbb{G}(1,r)\dashrightarrow{\rm Sym}^{d}\mathbb{P}^{1}//SL_{2}\cong\overline{\mathcal{M}_{0,d}}/S_{d} $$

that sends each line $\ell\subset\mathbb{P}^{r}$ to the moduli of the $d$ unordered points $\ell\cap X$ on $\ell\cong\mathbb{P}^{1}$ ?

When $r=2$ , the answer to Problem 12.1 was shown to be 420 in [13]. We give a separate approach that yields the answer for all $r$ . More generally, in the threshold $d\geq 2r-2$ where a general such $X$ contains no lines, we find the class of a general fiber of $\phi_{X}$ in $\mathbb{G}(1,r)$ .

We can also ask a related question.

#### Problem 12.2.

With the setup of Problem 12.1, when $r=2$ Cadman and Laza [13] show

$$ \displaystyle\deg(\phi_{X})=2\cdot(\text{\# bitangents of $X$})+4\cdot(\text{\# flexes of $X$})=2\cdot 120+4\cdot 45=420. $$

How does this generalize to arbitrary $r$ ?

We solve Problem 12.1 in Theorem 12.5 and answer Problem 12.2 in Section 12.3.

### 12.1. Connection with $\mathcal{O}_{M}$

For the rest of Section 12, all of our cycles $\mathcal{O}_{M}$ are in a product of $\mathbb{P}^{1}$ ’s. For any matrix $M$ , denote by $(\mathcal{O}_{M})_{\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{S}^{\vee})^{d}}$ the pullback of $\mathcal{O}_{M}$ from $\mathbb{P}(\zeta_{2})^{d}$ , where $\zeta_{2}$ is the universal rank $2$ vector bundle. By an abuse of notation, we will drop the subscript $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{S}^{\vee})^{d}$ when it is clear from context.

#### Lemma 12.3.

Let $f$ be a homogeneous form of degree $d$ on $K^{r+1}$ such that $X=V(f)\subset\mathbb{P}^{r}$ contains no lines. Denoting by $\mathcal{S}$ the tautological bundle on $\mathbb{G}(1,r)$ , there is an everywhere nonzero section $\mathbb{G}(1,r)\to{\rm Sym}^{d}\mathcal{S}^{\vee}$ induced by $f$ , and the class of the image of the induced section $s:\mathbb{G}(1,r)\to\mathbb{P}({\rm Sym}^{d}\mathcal{S}^{\vee})$ is given by

$$ \displaystyle[{\rm im}(s)]=H^{d}+c_{1}({\rm Sym}^{d}\mathcal{S}^{\vee})H^{d-1}+\cdots+c_{d}({\rm Sym}^{d}\mathcal{S}^{\vee}). $$

#### Proof.

Let $V=K^{r+1}$ . Then, the canonical inclusion of $\mathcal{S}\subset V\times\mathbb{G}(1,V)$ of vector bundles over $\mathbb{G}(1,V)$ induces a surjection ${\rm Sym}^{d}(V^{\vee})\times\mathbb{G}(1,V)\to{\rm Sym}^{d}(\mathcal{S}^{\vee})$ of vector bundles. The section $\mathbb{G}(1,V)\to{\rm Sym}^{d}\mathcal{S}^{\vee}$ is the composition

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{G}(1,V)\to{\rm Sym}^{d}(V^{\vee})\times\mathbb{G}(1,V)\to{\rm Sym}^{d}\mathcal{S}^{\vee}. $$

If $X=V(f)$ contains no lines, then $f$ restricts to something nonzero on each line, so $\mathbb{G}(1,V)\to{\rm Sym}^{d}\mathcal{S}^{\vee}$ avoids zero. The formula for $[{\rm im}(s)]$ follows from [20, Proposition 9.13]. ∎

Lemma 12.4 describes the class of a general fiber of $\phi_{X}$ , and contains a rigorous definition of $\phi_{X}$ in its proof.

#### Lemma 12.4.

With the setup of Lemma 12.3, assume every line in $\mathbb{P}^{r}$ meets $X$ in at least three points. The general fiber of

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{X}:\mathbb{G}(1,r)\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}({\rm Sym}^{d}(K^{\vee})^{2})//SL_{2} $$

is closed in $\mathbb{G}(1,r)$ and has class $s^{*}\Phi_{*}[\mathcal{O}_{M}]_{\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{S}^{\vee})^{d}}$ , where $M$ is a general $2\times d$ matrix and $\Phi$ is the multiplication map

$$ \displaystyle\Phi:\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{S}^{\vee})^{d}\to\mathbb{P}({\rm Sym}^{d}\mathcal{S}^{\vee}), $$

where $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{S}^{\vee})^{d}$ denotes the $d$ -fold fiber product of $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{S}^{\vee})$ with itself over $\mathbb{G}(1,r)$ .

#### Proof.

Let $U\subset\mathbb{G}(1,r)$ be an open subset over which $\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{G}(1,r)$ is trivial. Taking a trivialization, we have an $SL_{2}$ -equivariant map $\mathbb{P}({\rm Sym^{d}}\mathcal{S}^{\vee})|_{U}\to U$ . We can take the GIT quotient, which gives us

Given another open subset $U^{\prime}\subset\mathbb{G}(1,r)$ over which $\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{G}(1,r)$ is trivial, we get identifications of the GIT quotients over $U\cap U^{\prime}$ that are independent of the trivializations chosen over $U$ and $U^{\prime}$ .

This means the GIT quotients over each $U$ glue together to a global object, and this global object is precisely $\mathbb{G}(1,r)\times(\mathbb{P}({\rm Sym}^{d}(K^{\vee})^{2})//SL_{2})$ . We have an induced map

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}({\rm Sym^{d}}\mathcal{S}^{\vee})\dashrightarrow\mathbb{G}(1,r)\times(\mathbb{P}({\rm Sym}^{d}(K^{\vee})^{2})//SL_{2})\to\mathbb{P}({\rm Sym}^{d}(K^{\vee})^{2})//SL_{2} $$

and the map $\phi_{X}$ can be defined as the composite

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{X}:\mathbb{G}(1,r)\xrightarrow{s}\mathbb{P}({\rm Sym^{d}}\mathcal{S}^{\vee})\dashrightarrow\mathbb{G}(1,r)\times(\mathbb{P}({\rm Sym}^{d}(K^{\vee})^{2})//SL_{2})\to\mathbb{P}({\rm Sym}^{d}(K^{\vee})^{2})//SL_{2}. $$

Let $U_{s}\subset\mathbb{P}({\rm Sym^{d}}\mathcal{S}^{\vee})$ denote the dense open subset of points that are stable with respect to the local GIT quotients above. The set $U_{s}$ consists of configurations of $d$ points on a line such that no point with multiplicity at least $\frac{d}{2}$ appears. The map (9) is defined on $U_{s}$ and maps a stable configuration of $d$ points to the class of its $SL_{2}$ orbit in $\mathbb{P}({\rm Sym}^{d}(K^{\vee})^{2})//SL_{2}$ . A general fiber of the map $U_{s}\to\mathbb{P}({\rm Sym}^{d}(K^{\vee})^{2})//SL_{2}$ given by (9) is $\Phi_{*}\mathcal{O}_{M}\cap U_{s}$ .

The set $s^{-1}(U_{s})$ is in the domain of definition of $\phi_{X}$ , and the scheme $s^{-1}(\Phi_{*}\mathcal{O}_{M}\cap U_{s})$ is a general fiber of $\phi_{X}$ restricted to $s^{-1}(U_{s})$ . We claim that

$$ \displaystyle s(\mathbb{G}(1,r))\cap\Phi_{*}\mathcal{O}_{M}\subset U_{s}. $$

Indeed, every configuration in the boundary of $\Phi_{*}\mathcal{O}_{M}$ (supported on fewer than $d$ points) must be supported on at most 2 points for dimension reasons, and thus ${\rm im}(s)$ does not intersect the boundary of $\Phi_{*}\mathcal{O}_{M}$ by assumption. Since the complement of the boundary of $\Phi_{*}\mathcal{O}_{M}$ lies in $U_{s}$ , we have $s(\mathbb{G}(1,r))\cap\Phi_{*}\mathcal{O}_{M}\subset U_{s}$ .

Therefore, $s^{-1}(\Phi_{*}\mathcal{O}_{M}\cap U_{s})=s^{-1}(\Phi_{*}\mathcal{O}_{M})$ , which completes the proof. ∎

### 12.2. Computation of degree

#### Theorem 12.5.

Let $X\subset\mathbb{P}^{r}$ be a hypersurface of degree $d$ such that every line meets $X$ in at least three points and is not contained in $X$ . After restricting the rational map

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{X}:\mathbb{G}(1,r)\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}({\rm Sym}^{d}(K^{\vee})^{2})//SL_{2} $$

to its domain of definition, the general fiber is closed in $\mathbb{G}(1,r)$ and has class

$$ \displaystyle d(d-1)(d-2)\prod_{k=2}^{d-2}(ku+(d-k)v), $$

where $u,v$ are the Chern roots of the dual $\mathcal{S}^{\vee}\to\mathbb{G}(1,r)$ of the tautological bundle. In particular, if $d=2r+1$ , then the degree of $\phi_{X}$ is the difference between the coefficients of $u^{r-1}v^{r-1}$ and $u^{r-2}v^{r}$ in the expansion of $d(d-1)(d-2)\prod_{k=2}^{d-2}(ku+(d-k)v)$ .

#### Example 2.

For $(d,r)=(7,3)$ , we are considering line sections of a degree $7$ surface in $\mathbb{P}^{3}$ . Theorem 12.5 says the degree in this case is 77070.

#### Proof.

Let $M$ be a general $2\times d$ matrix. By Lemma 12.4, the class of a general fiber of $\phi_{X}$ is $s^{*}\Phi_{*}[\mathcal{O}_{M}]_{\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{S}^{\vee})^{d}}$ .

By the projection formula, we have

$$ \displaystyle s^{*}\Phi_{*}[\mathcal{O}_{M}]_{\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{S}^{\vee})^{d}}=(\pi_{2})_{*}s_{*}(s^{*}\Phi_{*}[\mathcal{O}_{M}]_{\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{S}^{\vee})^{d}}) \displaystyle=(\pi_{2})_{*}(s_{*}[\mathbb{G}(1,r)]\cap\Phi_{*}[\mathcal{O}_{M}]_{\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{S}^{\vee})^{d}}) \displaystyle=(\pi_{2})_{*}\Phi_{*}(\Phi^{*}s_{*}[\mathbb{G}(1,r)]\cap[\mathcal{O}_{M}]_{\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{S}^{\vee})^{d}}) \displaystyle=(\pi_{1})_{*}(\Phi^{*}[{\rm im}(s)]\cap[\mathcal{O}_{M}]_{\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{S}^{\vee})^{d}}). $$

To compute $(\pi_{1})_{*}(\Phi^{*}[{\rm im}(s)]\cap[\mathcal{O}_{M}]_{\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{S}^{\vee})^{d}})$ , we will use Lemma 12.3 and Section 10.2.

Let $F(z)=(z+u)(z+v)$ be the Leray relation of $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{S}^{\vee})$ , let

$$ G(z)=\prod_{k=0}^{d}(z+ku+(d-k)v)=z^{d+1}+c_{1}({\rm Sym}^{d}\mathcal{S}^{\vee})z^{d}+\cdots+c_{d+1}({\rm Sym}^{d}\mathcal{S}^{\vee}) $$

be the Leray relation of $\mathbb{P}({\rm Sym}^{d}\mathcal{S}^{\vee})$ and let $H=\mathscr{O}_{\mathbb{P}({\rm Sym}^{d}\mathcal{S}^{\vee})}(1)$ . By Lemma 12.3, we have $[{\rm im}(s)]=L(H)$ , where $L$ is the polynomial

$$ L(z)=\frac{G(z)-G(0)}{z}. $$

Hence $\Phi^{*}[{\rm im}(s)]=L(\sum_{i=1}^{d}H_{i})$ , where $H_{i}$ denotes $\mathscr{O}_{\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{S}^{\vee})}(1)$ pulled back from the $i$ th factor.

Let $\overline{L}(H_{1},\ldots,H_{d})$ be the result of reducing $L(\sum_{i=1}^{d}H_{i})$ modulo $F(H_{i})=(H_{i}+u)(H_{i}+v)$ for each $i$ . Then by Section 10.2 we have

$$ \pi_{*}(\Phi^{*}[{\rm im}(s)]\cap[\mathcal{O}_{M}]_{\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{S}^{\vee})^{d}})=[z^{1}][F(z)^{1}]\overline{L}(z,\ldots,z). $$

(As usual, $[F(z)^{1}]\overline{L}(z,\ldots,z)$ denotes the coefficient $a_{1}$ when $\overline{L}(z,\ldots,z)$ is expressed as $a_{0}(z)+a_{1}(z)F(z)+a_{2}F(z)^{2}+\cdots$ , where each $a_{i}$ is a polynomial of degree at most $1$ in $z$ .)

We can thus carry out the computation of the class of the general fiber of $\phi_{X}$ in three steps: first we compute $\overline{L}(H_{1},\ldots,H_{n})$ , second we compute $\overline{L}(z,\ldots,z)$ , and third we compute the answer $[z^{1}][F(z)^{1}]\overline{L}(z,\ldots,z)$ . We will perform these steps completely formally, treating all variables as indeterminates with no relations between them, i.e. in the ring $\mathbb{Q}(u,v,H_{1},\ldots,H_{n},z)$ . In particular, we will not use any relations between the $H_{i}$ and $u,v$ in the relevant Chow rings.

Step 1 Note that $\overline{L}(H_{1},\ldots,H_{n})$ has degree at most $1$ in each $H_{i}$ and agrees with $L(\sum_{i=1}^{d}H_{i})$ on $\{-u,-v\}^{d}$ . Hence we may compute $\overline{L}(H_{1},\ldots,H_{n})$ by evaluating $L(\sum_{i=1}^{d}H_{i})$ on $\{-u,-v\}^{d}$ and using the Lagrange interpolation formula. Observe that the term $G(H_{1}+\ldots+H_{d})$ of

$$ L(H_{1}+\ldots+H_{d})=\frac{G(H_{1}+\ldots+H_{d})-G(0)}{H_{1}+\ldots+H_{d}} $$

vanishes on $\{-u,-v\}^{d}$ , so we get

$$ \overline{L}(H_{1},\ldots,H_{n})=\sum_{T\subset\{1,\ldots,d\}}\frac{-G(0)}{-|T|v-(d-|T|)u}\left(\prod_{i\in T}\frac{H_{i}+u}{-v+u}\right)\left(\prod_{i\in\{1,\ldots,d\}\setminus T}\frac{H_{i}+v}{-u+v}\right). $$

Step 2 Substituting $z$ for each $H_{i}$ yields

$$ \displaystyle\overline{L}(z,\ldots,z) \displaystyle=G(0)\sum_{k=0}^{d}\frac{1}{kv+(d-k)u}\binom{d}{k}\frac{(z+u)^{k}(z+v)^{d-k}}{(u-v)^{k}(v-u)^{d-k}} \displaystyle=\frac{G(0)}{(u-v)^{d}}\sum_{k=0}^{d}\frac{\binom{d}{k}(z+u)^{k}(-z-v)^{d-k}}{kv+(d-k)u} $$

Step 3 All terms of (10) except for the $k=0,1,d-1,d$ terms are divisible by $F(z)^{2}$ . Thus

$$ \displaystyle[z^{1}][F(z)^{1}]\overline{L}(z,\ldots,z) \displaystyle=\frac{G(0)}{(u-v)^{d}}[z^{1}][F(z)^{1}] \displaystyle\left(\frac{(-z-v)^{d}}{du}+\frac{d(z+u)(-z-v)^{d-1}}{v+(d-1)u}\right. \displaystyle\left.+\frac{d(z+u)^{d-1}(-z-v)}{(d-1)v+u}+\frac{(z+u)^{d}}{dv}\right) \displaystyle=\frac{G(0)}{(u-v)^{d}}[z^{1}][F(z)^{1}] \displaystyle\left(\frac{(-1)^{d}(z+v)^{d}}{du}+\frac{(-1)^{d-1}dF(z)(z+v)^{d-2}}{v+(d-1)u}\right. \displaystyle\left.-\frac{dF(z)(z+u)^{d-2}}{(d-1)v+u}+\frac{(z+u)^{d}}{dv}\right). $$

We note now that

$$ \displaystyle(z+u)^{k}\equiv \displaystyle(z+u)(u-v)^{k-1} \displaystyle+F(z)(-(z+v)(u-v)^{k-3}+(z+u)(k-1)(u-v)^{k-3})\pmod{F(z)^{2}}. $$

because both sides of the equation and their first derivatives agree on $\{-u,-v\}$ . Hence

$$ \displaystyle[z^{1}][F(z)^{1}]F(z)(z+u)^{k} \displaystyle=(u-v)^{k-1},\qquad[z^{1}][F(z)^{1}](z+u)^{k} \displaystyle=(k-2)(u-v)^{k-3}, \displaystyle[z^{1}][F(z)^{1}]F(z)(z+v)^{k} \displaystyle=(v-u)^{k-1},\qquad[z^{1}][F(z)^{1}](z+v)^{k} \displaystyle=(k-2)(v-u)^{k-3}. $$

Applying this term by term to (11), we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\phantom{=}\frac{G(0)}{(u-v)^{d}}\left(-\frac{(d-2)(u-v)^{d-3}}{du}+\frac{d(u-v)^{d-3}}{v+(d-1)u}-\frac{d(u-v)^{d-3}}{(d-1)v+u}+\frac{(d-2)(u-v)^{d-3}}{dv}\right) \displaystyle=G(0)\frac{(d-1)(d-2)}{du(u+(d-1)v)((d-1)v+u)v} \displaystyle=d(d-1)(d-2)\prod_{k=2}^{d-2}(ku+(d-k)v), $$

which finishes the proof in general. In the case $d=2r+1$ , the degree of $\phi_{X}$ is the $u^{r}v^{r}$ term when we decompose our expression into Schubert cycles, which are Schur polynomials in the Chern roots $u,v$ of $\mathcal{S}^{\vee}$ [24, Chapter 10, Proposition 8]. This is the difference between the $u^{r-1}v^{r-1}$ coefficient and the $u^{r-2}v^{r}$ coefficient of $d(d-1)(d-2)\prod_{k=2}^{d-2}(ku+(d-k)v)$ . ∎

### 12.3. Degeneration of the general orbit

We now answer Problem 12.2, generalizing the relation in the case $r=2$ to arbitrary $r$ , via a relation between generalized matrix orbit classes. The following definition will be used in Section 12.3 only.

#### Definition 12.1.

Given a partition $A_{1}\sqcup\ldots\sqcup A_{k}$ of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ , let $M_{A_{1}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup A_{k}}$ denote a choice of a $2\times n$ matrix such that two columns are linearly dependent if and only if their indices lie in the same $A_{i}$ . Equivalently, we may define

$$ M_{A_{1}\sqcup\ldots\sqcup A_{k}}=\tau^{\leq 2}(\tau^{\leq 1}(\oplus_{j\in A_{1}}\ast)\oplus\ldots\oplus\tau^{\leq 1}(\oplus_{j\in A_{k}}\ast)). $$

By Theorem 7.1, the class $[\mathcal{O}_{M_{A_{1}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup A_{k}}}]$ depends only on the partition $A_{1}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup A_{k}$ and not on the specific choice of $M_{A_{1}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup A_{k}}$ .

#### Proposition 12.6.

We have

$$ \displaystyle[\mathcal{O}_{M_{\{1\}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup\{n\}}}]=\sum_{i=1}^{n-2}{[\mathcal{O}_{M_{\{1,\ldots,i\}\sqcup\{i+1\}\sqcup\{i+2,\ldots,n\}}}]} $$

#### Proof.

This follows by Theorem 7.1 and the subdivision of Schubert rank polytopes in the proof of Theorem 8.2. This also follows from an application of [35, Theorem 1.3.6] in the case where interior vertices of our tree form a chain. Not coincidentially, in characteristic zero, this also follows from Section 4.4. ∎

As a corollary of Proposition 12.6, we have

#### Theorem 12.7.

With the setup of Lemma 12.3, if $d=2r+1$ , then the degree of $\phi_{X}$ is

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{a\geq b>1,a+b+1=d}{2n_{a,b,1}}+4n_{d-2,1,1}, $$

where

$$ n_{a,b,c}=\int_{\mathbb{G}(1,r)}s^{*}[\overline{Z_{a,b,c}}] $$

and $Z_{a,b,c}\subset{\rm Sym}^{d}(\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{S}^{\vee}))=\mathbb{P}({\rm Sym}^{d}\mathcal{S}^{\vee})$ is the closure of the locus of $n$ -tuples of points in each fiber supported at $3$ points with multiplicities $a,b,c$ .

#### Remark 12.8.

The inverse image $s^{-1}(Z_{a,b,c})$ consists exactly of lines that intersect $X$ at three points with multiplicities exactly $a,b,c$ . Hence, we may think of $n_{a,b,c}$ as the number of such lines, counted with multiplicity. In characteristic zero, it is possible to give a transversality argument to show that, for a general $X$ , we can take $n_{a,b,c}$ to be the honest number of lines, as all lines appear with multiplicity one.

#### Proof.

By Lemma 12.4, the degree of $\phi_{X}$ is equal to the degree of $s^{*}\Phi_{*}[\mathcal{O}_{M_{\{1\}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup\{d\}}}]$ , where

$$ \displaystyle\Phi:\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{S}^{\vee})^{d}\to\mathbb{P}({\rm Sym}^{d}\mathcal{S}^{\vee}) $$

is the multiplication map. By Proposition 12.6, we have

$$ \displaystyle s^{*}\Phi_{*}[\mathcal{O}_{M_{\{1\}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup\{d\}}}]=\sum_{i=1}^{d-2}s^{*}\Phi_{*}[\mathcal{O}_{M_{\{1,\ldots,i\}\sqcup\{i+1\}\sqcup\{i+2,\ldots,d\}}}]. $$

Now, observe that $\Phi$ maps $\mathcal{O}_{M_{\{1,\ldots,i\}\sqcup\{i+1\}\sqcup\{i+2,\ldots,d\}}}$ generically two-to-one onto $\overline{Z_{i,d-i-1,1}}$ if $i\in\{1,\frac{d-1}{2},d-2\}$ and birationally onto it otherwise. Therefore $s^{*}\Phi_{*}[\mathcal{O}_{M_{\{1,\ldots,i\}\sqcup\{i+1\}\sqcup\{i+2,\ldots,d\}}}]$ is the class of $2n_{i,d-i-1,1}$ points if $i\in\{1,\frac{d-1}{2},d-2\}$ and $n_{i,d-i-1,1}$ points otherwise. Taking the sum from $i=1$ to $d-2$ yields the desired answer. ∎

#### Remark 12.9.

Using the properties of $[M]_{\hbar}$ in Section 10 and the description of $M_{A_{1}\sqcup\ldots\sqcup A_{k}}$ in terms of truncations and direct sums with $\ast$ , one can compute the $n_{a,b,1}$ directly.

## 13. Lifting to $\mathbb{A}^{(r+1)\times n}$

In this section, we show that our formulas for $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ and $[\overline{\Gamma_{M}}]$ allow us to compute the $GL_{r+1}\times(K^{\times})^{n}$ -equivariant classes of the analogues of $\mathcal{O}_{M}$ and $\overline{\Gamma_{M}}$ in $\mathbb{A}^{(r+1)\times n}$ , thus completing and vastly extending the computation of Berget and Fink in [9]. The precise formulation of the problem for $\mathcal{O}_{M}$ is as follows.

#### Problem 13.1.

Let $T=(K^{\times})^{n}$ be the torus. We have a $GL_{r+1}\times T$ -equivariant analogue

$$ \displaystyle{\rm mult}_{M}:\mathbb{A}^{(r+1)\times d}\times_{K^{\times}}T\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{(r+1)\times n} $$

of $\mu_{M}$ that sends $(A,D)\in\mathbb{A}^{(r+1)\times d}\times_{K^{\times}}T$ to the product $AMD$ . What is the class of the image closure of ${\rm mult}_{M}$ in $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}\times T}(\mathbb{A}^{(r+1)\times n})$ as an $((r+1)d+n-1)$ -dimensional cycle?

By Corollary 13.3 below, the formula in Theorem 9.1 for $[\mathcal{O}_{M}]$ is precisely the same as the formula for the lifted class described in Problem 13.1, as it satisfies a certain degree bound of Fehér and Rimányi [22]. This formula works verbatim even if $M$ has zero columns because the locus of matrices with vanishing $i$ th column has class $F(H_{i})$ . We can also lift $[\overline{\Gamma_{M}}]$ in an analogous fashion because the formula in Theorem 11.1 satisfies the degree bounds.

### 13.1. Degree bound of Fehér and Rimányi

To pass from

$$ \displaystyle A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}\times T}(\mathbb{A}^{(r+1)\times n})\cong\mathbb{Z}[t_{0},\ldots,t_{r}]^{S_{r+1}}[H_{1},\ldots,H_{n}] $$

to $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}}((\mathbb{P}^{r})^{n})$ , we remove the locus in $\mathbb{A}^{(r+1)\times n}$ of matrices containing a zero column and quotient out by the resulting free $T$ -action. This amounts to taking the quotient of $A^{\bullet}_{GL_{r+1}\times T}(\mathbb{A}^{(r+1)\times n})$ by the ideal generated by $F(H_{i})$ for $1\leq i\leq n$ .

#### Lemma 13.2 ([22, Theorem 2.1]).

Let $V_{1},V_{2}$ be vector spaces and let $G$ be an algebraic group that acts on $V_{1}\oplus V_{2}$ . Let $K^{\times}$ act on $V_{1}$ trivially and on $V_{2}$ by scaling. Let $X\subset V_{1}\oplus V_{2}$ be an irreducible closed $G\times K^{\times}$ -invariant subvariety not contained in $V_{1}$ .

Then, under the isomorphism $A_{G\times K^{\times}}^{\bullet}(V_{1}\oplus V_{2})\cong A_{G}^{\bullet}({\rm pt})\otimes\mathbb{Z}[H]$ , the class $[X]$ maps to an expression $\sum x_{j}\otimes H^{j}$ where $x_{j}=0$ if $j\geq\dim(V_{2})$ .

#### Proof.

This is a special case of the argument in [22, Theorem 2.1] applied to the case $V=V_{1}$ , $V^{\#}=V_{1}\oplus V_{2}$ , $G=G$ , $H=K^{\times}$ , $\eta^{\#}=X$ , and $\eta=X\cap V_{1}$ . Since the argument is short and our setting is with equivariant Chow groups instead of equivariant cohomology, we recall the proof for completeness.

Consider the diagram

The class $\sum x_{j}\otimes H^{j}$ maps to zero in $A_{G\times K^{\times}}^{\bullet}((V_{1}\oplus V_{2})\backslash X)$ , so the image of $\sum x_{i}\otimes H^{j}$ in $A_{G\times K^{\times}}^{\bullet}(V_{1})$ is in the kernel of $A_{G\times K^{\times}}^{\bullet}(V_{1})\to A_{G\times K^{\times}}^{\bullet}(V_{1}\backslash(X\cap V_{1}))$ . In particular, this means that each $x_{j}$ is in the kernel of $A_{G\times K^{\times}}^{\bullet}(V_{1})\to A_{G\times K^{\times}}^{\bullet}(V_{1}\backslash(X\cap V_{1}))$ .

Since $X$ is irreducible and not contained in $V_{1}$ , we have $\dim(X\cap V_{1})\leq\dim(X)-1$ , or equivalently, the codimension of $X\cap V_{1}$ in $V_{1}$ is at most the codimension of $X$ in $V_{1}\oplus V_{2}$ minus $(\dim(V_{2})-1)$ . If $j\geq\dim(V_{2})$ , then the codimension of $x_{j}$ is at most the codimension of $X$ in $V_{1}\oplus V_{2}$ minus $\dim(V_{2})$ . Since it is in the kernel of $A_{G\times K^{\times}}^{\bullet}(V_{1})\to A_{G\times K^{\times}}^{\bullet}(V_{1}\backslash(X\cap V_{1}))$ , it must be zero. ∎

#### Corollary 13.3.

Let $G$ be an algebraic group and let $V_{1},\ldots,V_{n}$ be representations of $G$ . Let $T=(K^{\times})^{n}$ act on $V_{1}\oplus\cdots\oplus V_{n}$ by scaling each summand separately.

Let $X\subset V_{1}\times\cdots\times V_{n}$ be an irreducible closed $G\times T$ -invariant subvariety intersecting $(V_{1}\backslash\{0\})\times\cdots\times(V_{n}\backslash\{0\})$ and let $f$ be a polynomial with coefficients in $A^{\bullet}_{G}({\rm pt})$ such that $f(H_{1},\ldots,H_{n})$ is the class

$$ \displaystyle[X\cap(V_{1}\backslash\{0\})\times\cdots\times(V_{n}\backslash\{0\})] \displaystyle\in A_{G\times T}^{\bullet}((V_{1}\backslash\{0\})\times\cdots\times(V_{n}\backslash\{0\})) \displaystyle=A_{G}^{\bullet}(\mathbb{P}(V_{1})\times\cdots\times\mathbb{P}(V_{n})) \displaystyle=A_{G}^{\bullet}({\rm pt})[H_{1},\ldots,H_{n}]/(p_{V_{1}}(H_{1}),\ldots,p_{V_{n}}(H_{n})), $$

where $p_{V}(z)=z^{\dim V}+c_{1}^{G}(V)z^{\dim V-1}+\ldots+c_{\dim V}^{G}(V)$ denotes the Leray relation of $V$ .

Assume that $f$ has degree less than $\dim(V_{i})$ in each $H_{i}$ . Then the class

$$ [X]\in A^{\bullet}_{G\times T}(V_{1}\times\cdots\times V_{n})=A^{\bullet}_{G}({\rm pt})[H_{1},\ldots,H_{n}] $$

is equal to $f(H_{1},\ldots,H_{n})$ .

#### Proof.

The result follows from a repeated application of Lemma 13.2. ∎

Hence, the formulas in 9.1 and 11.1 solve Problem 13.1.

## Appendix A Polytopes

We collect here facts about (convex) polytope geometry and matroid polytopes that we need in the body of the paper. Not all polytopes we will work with are bounded.

#### Definition A.1.

Say $P$ is a cone if $|{\operatorname{Vert}}(P)|\leq 1$ . Equivalently, $P$ is the Minkowski sum of a point $v$ and rays $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v_{i}$ . If such a cone does not contain a line, then $v$ is the unique vertex of the cone, called its apex.

If a cone $v+\sum_{i}\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v_{i}$ has an apex, then its edges are a subset of the rays $v+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v_{i}$ .

#### Definition A.2.

The tangent cone of a polytope $P$ at a point $p\in P$ is

$$ T_{p,P}=p+\bigcup_{p^{\prime}\in P}\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}(p^{\prime}-p). $$

If the polytope $P$ is understood, we will denote the tangent cone simply by $T_{p}$ . There exists a finite set $S\subset P$ such that $T_{p}=p+\sum_{p^{\prime}\in S}\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}(p^{\prime}-p)$ , so $T_{p}$ a polytope and a cone.

An equivalent description of $x\in P$ to be a vertex is that $T_{x}$ contains no line.

Given polytopes $P$ , $Q$ , and points $p\in P$ , $q\in Q$ , we have $T_{p+q,P+Q}=T_{p,P}+T_{q,Q}$ . As the sum of cones which contain lines is a cone which contains lines, we have

$$ {\operatorname{Vert}}(P+Q)=\{x+y\mid x\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(P),y\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(Q),T_{x}+T_{y}\text{ does not contain a line}\}. $$

More generally, every face of $P+Q$ is the Minkowski sum of a face of $P$ with a face of $Q$ .

The following is an equivalent characterization of rank polytopes arising from matroids (not necessarily arising from matrices).

#### Lemma A.1.

[28] A polytope $P\subset\Delta$ is the rank polytope of a matroid if and only if ${\operatorname{Vert}}(P)\subset{\operatorname{Vert}}(\Delta)$ and all edges of $P$ are parallel to vectors of the form $e_{i}-e_{j}$ . In particular, every nonempty face of a rank polytope is also a rank polytope.

This is the only property of rank polytopes we will be using, and to emphasize this, in this section we work with matroids ${\mathcal{M}}$ and their rank polytopes $P_{\mathcal{M}}$ rather than with matrices.

#### Definition A.3.

We define a matroidal cone $C$ to be a cone with apex at the origin which is generated by rays of the form $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}(e_{i}-e_{j})$ . If $C$ is a matroidal cone generated by lines, we define the equivalence relation $\sim_{C}$ on $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ by $i\sim_{C}j$ if $e_{i}-e_{j}\in C$ and we call $C$ the associated cone to $\sim_{C}$ .

Note that if $C$ is a matroidal cone generated by lines, then

$$ C=\left\{(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\middle|\text{$\sum_{i\in S_{j}}x_{i}=0$ for all $j$}\right\}, $$

where $S_{1},\ldots,S_{k}$ are the equivalence classes of $\sim_{C}$ .

#### Corollary A.2.

Given a matroid ${\mathcal{M}}$ , there exists a unique partition $S_{1}\sqcup\ldots\sqcup S_{k}$ of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ such that $P_{\mathcal{M}}$ is a full-dimensional subset of

$$ T_{z}=\left\{(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\middle|\sum_{i\in S_{j}}x_{i}={\rm rk}_{{\mathcal{M}}}(S_{j})\text{ for all $j$}\right\} $$

for any relative interior point $z\in P_{\mathcal{M}}$ . In particular, for any point $(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in P_{\mathcal{M}}$ we have $\sum_{i\in S_{j}}x_{j}\in\mathbb{Z}$ for all $j$ .

#### Proof.

The tangent cone at $z$ is the Minkowski sum of the tangent cones of the vertices of $P_{\mathcal{M}}$ , so it is generated by some collection of vectors of the form $e_{i}-e_{j}$ and their negations. Now take $S_{1},\ldots,S_{k}$ to be the equivalence classes of $\sim_{T_{z}-z}$ . ∎

We will denote by $\sim_{{\mathcal{M}}}$ the equivalence relation $\sim_{T_{z}-z}$ for any relative interior point $z$ of $P_{\mathcal{M}}$ .

We are interested in polytopes of the form $P_{\mathcal{M}}+C$ for $C$ a matroidal cone and the intersections $(P_{\mathcal{M}}+C)\cap\Delta$ . We prove the key facts about these polytopes below. Recall that by abuse of notation we identify the vertices of $\Delta$ with $d$ -element subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ .

#### Lemma A.3.

Let ${\mathcal{M}}$ be a matroid and let $C$ be a matroidal cone. Then all edges of $P_{\mathcal{M}}+C$ are parallel to vectors of the form $e_{i}-e_{j}$ and $(P_{\mathcal{M}}+C)\cap\Delta$ is a matroid rank polytope with

$$ \displaystyle{\operatorname{Vert}}((P_{\mathcal{M}}+C)\cap\Delta)=\bigcup_{w\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(P_{\mathcal{M}})}(w+C)\cap{\operatorname{Vert}}(\Delta) \displaystyle=\{z\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(\Delta)\mid\exists w\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(P_{\mathcal{M}}),\text{bijection }\phi:z\setminus w\to w\setminus z\text{ with }e_{i}-e_{\phi(i)}\in C\ \forall i\} $$

#### Proof.

The edges of $P_{M}+C$ are parallel to vectors of the form $e_{i}-e_{j}$ by the results on Minkowski sums. We now prove (12) and (13), postponing the proof that $(P_{\mathcal{M}}+C)\cap\Delta$ is a matroid rank polytope until the end.

Suppose $z\in{\operatorname{Vert}}((P_{\mathcal{M}}+C)\cap\Delta)$ . Then there exists $w\in P_{\mathcal{M}}$ such that $w+\sum a_{\alpha}(e_{i_{\alpha}}-e_{j_{\alpha}})=z$ where each $a_{\alpha}>0$ and each $e_{i_{\alpha}}-e_{j_{\alpha}}\in C$ . Let $C^{\prime}=\sum_{\alpha}\mathbb{R}(e_{i_{\alpha}}-e_{j_{\alpha}})$ . Let ${\mathcal{M}}^{\prime}$ be the matroid such that $P_{{\mathcal{M}}^{\prime}}$ is the face of $P_{\mathcal{M}}$ that contains $w$ in its relative interior. Let $\sim_{{\mathcal{M}}^{\prime}+C^{\prime}}$ be the equivalence relation generated by $\sim_{{\mathcal{M}}^{\prime}}$ and $\sim_{C^{\prime}}$ . Then by the above $T_{z,P_{\mathcal{M}}+C}-z$ contains the associated cone of $\sim_{{\mathcal{M}}^{\prime}+C^{\prime}}$ .

By Corollary A.2, $w$ has integral sum of coordinates on any $\sim_{{\mathcal{M}}^{\prime}}$ equivalence class, and $z$ has the same sum of coordinates on any $\sim_{C^{\prime}}$ equivalence class as $w$ , so $z$ has integral sum of coordinates on any $\sim_{{\mathcal{M}}^{\prime}+C^{\prime}}$ -equivalence class.

We first show (12). Suppose $z_{i}\in(0,1)$ for some $i$ . Then there must exist an $i^{\prime}\sim_{{\mathcal{M}}^{\prime}+C^{\prime}}i$ with $i^{\prime}\neq i$ for which $z_{i^{\prime}}\in(0,1)$ . But then for sufficiently small $\epsilon>0$ , we have $z\pm\epsilon(e_{i}-e_{i^{\prime}})\in P_{\mathcal{M}}+C$ as $T_{z,P_{\mathcal{M}}+C}-z$ contains the associated cone of $\sim_{{\mathcal{M}}^{\prime}+C^{\prime}}$ . Also $z\pm\epsilon(e_{i}-e_{i^{\prime}})\in\Delta$ , so $z\pm\epsilon(e_{i}-e_{i^{\prime}})\in(P_{\mathcal{M}}+C)\cap\Delta,$ contradicting $z\in{\operatorname{Vert}}((P_{\mathcal{M}}+C)\cap\Delta)$ . Hence, $z\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(\Delta)$ .

Assume $w\in{\operatorname{Vert}}((z-C)\cap P_{\mathcal{M}})$ . We will now show that $w\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(P_{\mathcal{M}})$ (or equivalently $w\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(\Delta)$ ), which will complete the proof of (12).

It suffices to show that if $w\not\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(\Delta)$ , then $(T_{w,{\mathcal{M}}^{\prime}}-w)\cap C^{\prime}$ contains a nonzero vector $v$ . Indeed, such a $v$ yields a small linear perturbation $w\pm\epsilon v\in P_{\mathcal{M}}$ such that $w\pm\epsilon v\in z-C$ as well, contradicting that $w$ is a vertex of $(z-C)\cap P_{\mathcal{M}}$ .

If $w\not\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(\Delta)$ , then there exists $w_{i}\in(0,1)$ . Then since the sum of the coordinates of $w$ along any $\sim_{{\mathcal{M}}^{\prime}}$ -equivalence class is integral, there exists $i^{\prime}\sim_{{\mathcal{M}}^{\prime}}i$ with $i\neq i^{\prime}$ for which $w_{i^{\prime}}\in(0,1)$ . Similarly, since the sum of the coordinates of $z$ agrees with the sum of the coordinates of $w$ on any $\sim_{C^{\prime}}$ equivalence class, the sum of the coordinates of $w$ on any $\sim_{C^{\prime}}$ equivalence class is integral. Hence, there is an $i^{\prime\prime}\sim_{C^{\prime}}i^{\prime}$ with $i^{\prime\prime}\neq i^{\prime}$ for which $w_{i^{\prime}}\in(0,1)$ . Continuing in this fashion, we create a sequence of indices $i=i^{1},i^{2},\ldots$ for which $i^{2\beta-1}\sim_{C^{\prime}}i^{2\beta}$ are distinct and $i^{2\beta}\sim_{{\mathcal{M}}^{\prime}}i^{2\beta+1}$ are distinct and $w_{i^{\beta}}\in(0,1)$ for all $\beta$ . As the list of indices is finite, we have $i^{\alpha}=i^{\beta}$ for some minimal $\alpha<\beta$ . We may assume that $\alpha$ and $\beta$ have the same parity; otherwise, we replace $\alpha$ by $\alpha+1$ and $i^{\beta}$ by $i^{\alpha+1}$ . Now let

$$ v=\sum_{j=\alpha}^{\beta-1}(-1)^{j}e_{i^{j}}. $$

By grouping the terms in two different ways, we have $v\in T_{w,{\mathcal{M}}^{\prime}}-w$ and $v\in C^{\prime}$ as desired.

Hence $w\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(P_{\mathcal{M}})$ , completing the proof of (12).

By combining terms, we may assume that we never have $i_{\alpha}=j_{\alpha^{\prime}}$ in the equation. As $w,z\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(\Delta)$ , this then forces $j_{\alpha}\in w\setminus z$ and $i_{\alpha}\in z\setminus w$ . By Hall’s marriage theorem, some subset of $\{(j_{\alpha},i_{\alpha})\}$ yields a matching between $w\setminus z$ and $z\setminus w$ , demonstrating (13).

Finally, we show that $(P_{\mathcal{M}}+C)\cap\Delta$ is a matroid rank polytope. By (13), we can reach all of the vertices of $(P_{\mathcal{M}}+C)\cap\Delta$ by starting with $P_{\mathcal{M}}$ and applying the operation $P\mapsto(P+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v)\cap\Delta$ once for each $v$ of the form $e_{i}-e_{j}\in C$ . As it is clear that the result of applying this operation will keep $P$ contained inside $(P_{\mathcal{M}}+C)\cap\Delta$ , when we reach all of the vertices of $(P_{\mathcal{M}}+C)\cap\Delta$ we will have exactly the polytope $(P_{\mathcal{M}}+C)\cap\Delta$ . Hence, it suffices to show that the property of being a matroid rank polytope is preserved under $P\mapsto(P+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}(e_{i}-e_{j}))\cap\Delta$ . By (12), all vertices of $(P+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}(e_{i}-e_{j}))\cap\Delta$ are of the form $v+\lambda(e_{i}-e_{j})\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(\Delta)$ for $v\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(P)$ and $\lambda\geq 0$ . This forces either $\lambda=0$ , in which case $v+\lambda(e_{i}-e_{j})\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(P)$ , or $\lambda=1$ , in which case we get $(v\setminus j)\cup i$ whenever $j\in v$ and $i\not\in v$ . This description yields a matroid by the basis exchange property. ∎

#### Lemma A.4.

Let ${\mathcal{M}}$ be a matroid and let $C$ be a matroidal cone such that $P_{\mathcal{M}}=(P_{\mathcal{M}}+C)\cap\Delta$ . Let $v=e_{i}-e_{j}$ for some $i\neq j$ . Let $z$ be a vertex of $(P_{\mathcal{M}}+C+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v)\cap\Delta$ . Let $\lambda$ be the minimum nonnegative value such that $z-\lambda v\in P_{\mathcal{M}}+C$ , and let $\lambda^{\prime}$ be the minimum value of $|z\setminus w|$ over all pairs $(w,\phi)$ such that $w\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(P_{\mathcal{M}})$ and $\phi:z\setminus w\to w\setminus z$ is a bijection with $e_{k}-e_{\phi(k)}\in C+\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}v$ for all $k\in z\setminus w$ . Then $\lambda=\lambda^{\prime}$ .

#### Proof.

Lemma A.3 guarantees that $\lambda^{\prime}$ is well-defined. Observe that $z-w=\sum_{k\in z\setminus w}(e_{k}-e_{\phi(k)})$ . For each $k\in z\setminus w$ , we have either $e_{k}-e_{\phi(k)}\in C$ or $e_{k}-e_{\phi(k)}=v+(e_{k}-e_{i})+(e_{j}-e_{\phi(k)})\in v+C$ . Summing over all $k$ yields $z-w\in\mu v+C$ for some $\mu\leq|z\setminus w|=\lambda^{\prime}$ . Then $z-\mu v\in w+C\subset P_{\mathcal{M}}+C$ , so $\lambda\leq\mu\leq\lambda^{\prime}$ .

It remains to show that $\lambda^{\prime}\leq\lambda$ . We have an equation

$$ w+\sum_{\alpha}a_{\alpha}(e_{i_{\alpha}}-e_{j_{\alpha}})+\lambda v=z, $$

where $w\in P_{\mathcal{M}}$ and $a_{\alpha}>0$ and $e_{i_{\alpha}}-e_{j_{\alpha}}\in C$ for all $\alpha$ . Note that if $\lambda=0$ , then $z\in P_{\mathcal{M}}$ and we know that all coordinates of $z$ are integral so in fact $z\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(P_{\mathcal{M}})$ and the result is trivial. Hence, we may assume $\lambda>0$ .

We may assume our equation is reduced in the sense that $j_{\alpha}\neq i_{\beta}$ for any $\alpha\neq\beta$ . Let $C^{\prime}=\sum_{\alpha}\mathbb{R}(e_{i_{\alpha}}-e_{j_{\alpha}})$ . Clearly $e_{i}-e_{j}\not\in C^{\prime}$ (nor its negation) as then we could use this to decrease $\lambda$ by perturbing the equation. Hence, by reordering the indices, we may assume without loss of generality that $j_{\alpha}<i_{\alpha}$ and $j<i$ .

We may assume that $w\in P_{\mathcal{M}}$ is lexicographically maximal satisfying an equation of the form (14) with $j_{\alpha}<i_{\alpha}$ and $j<i$ .

We show first that $w\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(P_{\mathcal{M}})$ . As in the proof of Lemma A.3, if not all coordinates of $w$ are integral, then $(T_{w,{\mathcal{M}}}-w)\cap C^{\prime\prime}$ contains a line, where $C^{\prime\prime}$ is the cone generated by $\mathbb{R}(e_{i}-e_{j})$ and $\mathbb{R}(e_{i_{\alpha}}-e_{j_{\alpha}})$ for all $\alpha$ . If a nonzero multiple of $e_{i}-e_{j}$ is used in the expression for this line, then a small perturbation of $w$ along one of the two directions of the line decreases $\lambda$ , contradicting the minimality of $\lambda$ . Otherwise, $w$ may be perturbed in either direction, contradicting the lexicographic maximality of $w$ . Hence, $w\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(P_{\mathcal{M}})$ .

Suppose $\lambda$ is not integral. We have $i\sim_{C^{\prime}}j$ as otherwise the sum of the coordinates of the left-hand side of (14) in the $C^{\prime}$ -equivalence class containing $i$ is not an integer, contradicting the integrality of $z$ . Thus we may create a perturbation of the expression which decreases $\lambda$ , again a contradiction. Hence $\lambda$ is integral.

Suppose $a(e_{\ell}-e_{k})$ appears as one of the terms of the sum in (14) with $k\neq i,j$ and $\ell\neq i,j$ . Then for $0<\epsilon<a$ , we have $w+\epsilon(e_{l}-e_{k})\in P_{M}+C$ and $w+\epsilon(e_{l}-e_{k})\not\in P_{M}=(P_{M}+C)\cap\Delta$ by the lexicographic maximality of $w$ . Hence $w+\epsilon(e_{l}-e_{k})\not\in\Delta$ for $\epsilon$ arbitrarily small. This implies either $w_{l}=1$ or $w_{k}=0$ . No expression of the form $b(e_{k}-e_{k^{\prime}})$ appears in the sum, so if $w_{k}=0$ , then we have $w+\sum a_{\alpha}(e_{i_{\alpha}}-e_{j_{\alpha}})+\lambda(e_{i}-e_{j})$ has negative $k$ -coordinate, contradicting that $z\in\Delta$ . Similarly, no expression of the form $b(e_{\ell^{\prime}}-e_{\ell})$ appears in the sum, so if $w_{l}=1$ then we have $w+\sum_{\alpha}a_{\alpha}(e_{i_{\alpha}}-e_{j_{\alpha}})+\lambda(e_{i}-e_{j})$ has $\ell$ -coordinate strictly greater than $1$ , contradicting the assumption $z\in\Delta$ . Hence no such term $a(e_{\ell}-e_{k})$ appears in the sum.

Suppose now that $a(e_{\ell}-e_{j})$ appears as one of the terms of the sum in (14) with $\ell\neq i$ . Then by the same argument as above, either $w_{\ell}=1$ or $w_{j}=0$ lest $w$ not be lexicographically critical. If $w_{\ell}=1$ we argue as above, and if $w_{j}=0$ then since there is no other term in the sum of the form $b(e_{k}-e_{j})$ and $\lambda\geq 0$ , we get that $z_{j}<0$ , contradicting that $z\in\Delta$ . A similar argument shows that $a(e_{i}-e_{k})$ does not appear as one of the terms of the sum for $k\neq j$ .

Hence, each $e_{i_{\alpha}}-e_{j_{\alpha}}$ is of the form $e_{j}-e_{k}$ or $e_{\ell}-e_{i}$ . Since $w,z\in{\operatorname{Vert}}(\Delta)$ , we conclude that each $a_{\alpha}=1$ . Furthermore $w_{k}=1$ if a term of the form $e_{j}-e_{k}$ appears in the sum, and $w_{\ell}=0$ if a term of the form $e_{\ell}-e_{i}$ appears in the sum. Let $a$ be the number of terms of the form $e_{j}-e_{k}$ and let $b$ be the number of terms of the form $e_{l}-e_{i}$ . Then since $z_{i},z_{j}\in\{0,1\}$ , we conclude that $\lambda-1\leq a,b\leq\lambda+1$ . But $a=\lambda+1$ implies $a>0$ , so there is a term of the form $e_{j}-e_{k}$ , and it also implies $w_{j}=0$ , so $w+(e_{j}-e_{k})\in(P_{\mathcal{M}}+C)\cap\Delta=P_{\mathcal{M}}$ , contradicting the lexicographic maximality of $w$ . Thus $a\leq\lambda$ . Similarly, we have $b\leq\lambda$ . Combining the terms in the sum with $\lambda(e_{i}-e_{j})$ , we get $\lambda$ terms of the form $e_{i^{\prime}}-e_{j^{\prime}}\in C\cup(C+v)$ which yield a bijection $\phi:z\setminus w\to w\setminus z$ with $\phi(i^{\prime})=j^{\prime}$ . Hence $\lambda^{\prime}\leq\lambda$ as desired. ∎

## Appendix B Resolution via wonderful compactification

We recall the setup to blow up inductively an arrangement of subvarieties from [41]. In this section, a variety is a reduced irreducible scheme of finite type over $K$ .

### B.1. Arrangement of subvarieties

#### Definition B.1 ([41, Definition 2.1, Lemma 5.1]).

Let $X$ be a smooth variety and let $\mathcal{S}=\{S_{i}\}$ be a finite set of smooth nonempty proper subvarieties of $X$ . We say that $\mathcal{S}$ is a simple arrangment of subvarieties of $X$ if $\mathcal{S}\cup\{\emptyset\}$ is closed under scheme-theoretic intersection.

#### Definition B.2 ([41, Definition 2.2]).

Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a simple arrangement of subvarieties of $X$ . A subset $\mathcal{G}\subset\mathcal{S}$ is called a building set of $\mathcal{S}$ if for all $S\in\mathcal{S}$ , the minimal elements of $\mathcal{G}$ containing $S$ intersect transversely and their intersection is $S$ .

We say that a set $\mathcal{G}$ of subvarieties of $X$ is a building set if it is a building set of some simple arrangement $\mathcal{S}$ of subvarieties of $X$ . In this case $\mathcal{S}$ is the set of all proper nonempty intersections of elements of $\mathcal{G}$ .

### B.2. Wonderful compactification

#### Definition B.3 ([41, Definition 2.12]).

Let $X$ be a smooth variety and let $\mathcal{G}$ be a building set of subvarieties of $X$ . Order $\mathcal{G}=\{G_{1},\ldots,G_{n}\}$ so that $G_{i}\subset G_{j}$ implies $i<j$ , i.e. $G_{i}$ is a minimal element of $\{G_{i},\ldots,G_{n}\}$ for all $i$ . Let $X_{0}=X$ and for each $k$ with $0<k\leq n$ , let $X_{k}$ be the blowup of $X_{k-1}$ along $\widetilde{G_{k}}$ (the iterated strict transform of $G_{k}$ in $X_{k-1}$ ). Define the wonderful compactification $X_{\mathcal{G}}$ to be $X_{n}$ , which by Proposition B.2 below is independent of the ordering of $\mathcal{G}$ .

By [41, Proposition 2.8], all the blowups carried out in Definition B.3 have smooth centers, so $X_{\mathcal{G}}$ is smooth.

#### Remark B.1.

If $X$ carries the action of an algebraic group $G$ and $\mathcal{G}$ is a building set containing only $G$ -invariant subvarieties of $X$ , then the action of $G$ on $X$ induces an action of $G$ on $X_{\mathcal{G}}$ and the blowdown map $X_{\mathcal{G}}\to X$ is $G$ -equivariant.

#### Proposition B.2 ([41, Proposition 2.13]).

The construction of $X_{\mathcal{G}}$ in Definition B.3 agrees with the closure of the image

$$ \displaystyle X\backslash\bigcup_{G\in\mathcal{G}}G\hookrightarrow\prod_{G\in\mathcal{G}}{{\rm Bl}_{G}X}. $$

### B.3. Resolution of maps

Proposition B.2 allows one to resolve a collection of rational maps with smooth base loci via iterated blowups.

#### Proposition B.3.

Let $X\dashrightarrow X_{i}$ be a finite set of rational maps with simple base loci $B_{i}$ . If $\mathcal{G}$ is a building set of subvarieties of $X$ that contains each $B_{i}$ , then the wonderful compactification $X_{\mathcal{G}}\to X$ resolves the map $X\dashrightarrow\prod X_{i}$ .

#### Proof.

Consider the diagram

where the map $\prod_{G\in\mathcal{G}}{{\rm Bl}_{G}X}\to\prod_{i}{X_{i}}$ is given on each factor by the composition $\prod_{G\in\mathcal{G}}{{\rm Bl}_{G}X}\to{\rm Bl}_{B_{i}}X\to X_{i}$ . ∎

#### Corollary B.4.

Let $M$ be a $d\times n$ matrix with no zero columns. Let $V=K^{r}$ and let $W=K^{d}$ and let $x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\in W$ be the columns of $M$ . Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a building set of subvarieties of $\mathbb{P}^{(r+1)\times d-1}=\mathbb{P}(V\otimes W^{*})$ that contains each subspace $\mathbb{P}(V\otimes x_{i}^{\perp})$ . Then the wonderful compactification $B=(\mathbb{P}^{(r+1)\times d-1})_{\mathcal{G}}$ is a $GL_{r+1}$ -equivariant resolution of $\mu_{M}$ :

#### Proof.

Apply Proposition B.3 with $X=\mathbb{P}^{(r+1)\times d-1}$ and $X_{i}=\mathbb{P}^{r}$ , where the map $X\dashrightarrow X_{i}$ is the multiplication map by $x_{i}$ . The equivariance follows from Remark B.1. ∎
